This Company has been formed for the purpose of acquiring as a going concern, extending and carrying on : (a) The well known business formerly carried on by the Liverpool Patent Soap Comp% fly at Liverpool, together with their 13e,tish and Foreign P atents mud a large num- ber of valuable Trade Marks. (b) Allsights and interests in the celebrated Brand and Trade Mark " Titan " Patent Soap and the goodwill of same. (c) All rights and interest in a Patent granted to Thomas Arthur Myers 23554/93 in so far as same relates to the packing ot liquid soap, also (d) The extensive freehold property formerly known as Messrs. Medley and Sons' Soap Works, situate at 54 and 66, Naylor Street, Liverpool. amarrising 2,025 square yards of freehold land in one of the most desirable positions in the City of Liverpool and occupied by vain able Soap Works.

The object of the Company is to combine the aforesaid pro- perties and businesses and to manufacture and distribute the preaucts covered by tivi 0 micarty'a Pateats and Trade /larks and other reldive products (as occasion may offer) at home and abroad.

The Works ,tre Centrally situate, within six minutes walk of the Liverpool Exchange, close to the Goods Stations of the various Railway Companies, and in proximity to the line of Docks. They are capable of turning out 120 tons of soap per week.

The value of the properties acquired, and the extent. capacity, and suitability of the Works to the requirements of the Company's business may be gathered from the following Reports from Messrs. W. Niell and Son, Soap Makers' En- gineers and Experts, and Mr. NN Miami Thompson, Valuator. Liverpool, whose estimates show that a factory of similar character could not be erected and tilted to-day at a cost of less than £21.000.
W . NEILL & SON, bold Iron Works, St. Helens Junction, 12tri January. 1899. To IRE DIREOTO RS OF TITAN" SOAP. Lna-trirn, LiiriespeoL.

Dear Sirs,—its requested-Di-ion:We "vi..ited your works in Nayim Street, and, having inspected same, we estimate that the factory is Capable of turning out 123 tons of Soap per week, and estimate that a similar Works, exclusive of land, would, to-day, not cost loss than seventeen thousand pounds (say £17,000)4 Yours faithfully, W. To Tax DIRECTORS ' TITAN " SOAP, LIMITEID. GENTLEMEN.—As instructed I have inspeoted the piece of land, containing about 2,025 square yards. situate on the south side of Naylor-street, In the city of LLverpool, more particularly shown on the annexed sketch plan.
_ - The Tenure is stated to be Freehold and free from Chief Rent.

The property has been used for many years as a Soap Works, and I consider that the site is well suited for that purpose. I estimate the value of the above site, exclusive of Bul!slings. Plant and Machinery ereated thereon, at the sum of four thousand pounds (say £4,000). Yours truly, WM. THOMPSOM, Valuer and Property Auctioneer. The books show that the Customers' Acciunts are paid with promptitude, and there is au almost entire absence of bad debts.
MESSRS. VOISEY AKD WORTHINGTON, Chartered Account- ants, Warrington, report as follows :

21, King-street. Warrington, 27th January, 1899. To THE DIRECTORS " TiTIN " SoAP, LIMITED. CIENTLEMES,—We have ex,mined the bo,lis of the Liver- pool Patent Soap Company. and those relating to tbe manufacture of Titan" soap, tor three years ended 31st Decembim. 1897, and we certi4y that the net profits of the inanuiactrire and sate " Titan " Soap for that period have betni £15171 25 6d.—Yours truly. WORTHINGI4. The above is clear net profit after deducting every possible Charge, including the full expenditure for advertising.

During the year ending 318 t December, 1898 (for which period the books have not yet been au! ited), the average sales have not only been maintained, but the methods recently adopted tor banging the special qualities of Titan " Soap intimately under the notice of the consumers have resulted in a largely increased sale.

The Company has been fortunate in securing the services of Mr. F. 0. Kloninger, Ph.D., as Managaig Ditecter. Dr. Kloninger has been identified with the sucuss of the "Titan" Brand for luau years and his intimate acquaintance with the s cap industry in all its phases is a guarantee for the con- duct of the Company's business upon bounetsliues

There bsicg no Mortgage or Debenture Capital, the 5i per cent. Cumulative Preference Shares constitute a first claim (subject to the trade debts) on the entire assets, and are therefore an exceptionally well secured investuient.

rl he price to be paid by the Company for the various assets, Freehoid Properties, Patents, Maohinery.'Plant, TGols, Carts, itock-in-irtade (inoluang finished and unfinished goods), Stores. Furniture, Fittings &c.. is £18,030, payahle as to £30,000 in cash and the balance £lB, .00 (at the option of the Bit ectorß), in calls or in Pre erence Shares or in Ordinary Snares of tke Company or partly in Preference and partly in Ordinary Shares. The £17.0 0 remaining from the present issue will be BA aside for additiouid Working Capital and this, with the Capital already available, the DireeLirs con- sider to be arapiy sufficient. The Company take over the business as on the Ist January, 1899, including all profit f coin teat date.

LADIES' LETTER.

WY DEAR NELLIt, -- I have been struck this week with the very pretty toques that are coming into fashion for the spring, evidently. There was ono particularly I noticed, and that was a very stylish and servicable bat of fancy straw, trimmed with velvet and glace tucked silk in three graduated shades, and round the brim is a soft fold of lace, partly veiling the velvet. The large fan bow of silk at the left aide is tucked by machine, and in the centre is a knot of velvet, caught with a buckle. Under the brim at the left side is a pleating of the tucked silk in two shades, with a similar knot of velvet and a buckle. _ -

A new stylish little spring coat proves a very effective idea cf • arranging three-quarter inch 'braid, or, if two lines of I;r3.id are employed, the quarter-inch tubular kind is useful. The edge is -scalloped and braid sewn on, *gradually narrowing off to the waist, and then spreading out again on the bodice, If less el,i)nration is desired, lines eAn timply be arranged on,:e on the ft ou.t and on the rounded bank seinn9. The baPque is cu.t, to stand out well on the hip, and then draws in to ,the skirt. The front fastens with hooks and eyes, • and there arc •buttons at the bust and waiFlt only. The revers are made stiff, end faced wi!.!i velvet, leaving an edge of cloth, end tiie cothir, arranged in the seine rashion, is very 16tIg and also wired. A silk lining is absolutely necessary now that sleeves are worn tight, and a silk facing itnprom the front, if it cannot be used throliglieut.

A pretty dressing or toa-jacket is made of pale pink cloth trimmed with trills of cream lace which • edge the large square collar. Deep frills of the Same lace fall over the wrists, and the fronts are . rounded off in the usual fashion. This Matinita can be copied in nun's veiling, flannel or flan- nelette. A distipctive character in dress will certainly not be a "lack gown embroidered either in. steel or jet, with a deep fli,unce of lace at the hem, graduated towards the front, for that everybody has, ,but everybody has not as yet adopted the black lace girdles, nor the wreaths of flowers . placed on the shoulders which reach alines:: to the feet, It would hardly be a fur trimmed cat or cloak, especially if the fur chosen is chinchilla, for this is pretty well univQrsal wear, but it might be redeemed if the wearer chose to use the cigar brown, and had her OW° of velvet embroidered all over with steel and jet, made as a Priucesse. Nor must white cloth be need for either revers or cuffs, or as waistcoats or vests, for that everybody is wearing ; but this material is more •distinctive as an evening gown, and fa...,hion dictates that whips shall fiid a place on most dresses, and on nearly every kind of millinery, which is sudly over trimined.

If you are lucky enough in your exeni-cions to find a large pine cone—tne loigge.• the better—ripe and witle-open, seenre it: It wi!; form the basis of a pretty table decoration when flowers urn scarce and -Costly. Placa your none in a saiLler full of water, with the stein end of the cone nestkd in a mat of absorbent cut•ton, aml sprinkle coue and cotton thickly w!th in the dark until the seed bedris to ge,.ird7;ate, tlien bring into the sunlight. Turn it aruuoil now and then so that the sun may shine equal/y on all sides of your i cone, or t will not be EyminCtri;.:al, and keep the saucer supplied with water, aCtiling three drops of ammonia every day. In a few days you will have a living green cone which, if well cared fur, will last for weeks. Have you efer tried hot water for coughs. A wearying attack of coughing of ttli needs immediate attention, and that ewer-useiol remedy, hot water, will often do. good. It is Letter than the cough mixtures, which disorder trie digestion, and spoil the appetite. Water, almost boiling, should be Gipped when the par i oxysms come on.. A cough, resulting from irritation, s relieved by hot water through the promotion of secretion, which moistens the irritated surfaces. .Hot water also promotes expectoration, and so relieves the dry cough. Your loving JRNInn.

div.head: " WOMEYS CHAT."
div.p: " WOMEYS CHAT."

Nearly all the smartest women at the present time, are mothers ef daeghters either juatmr, or c3ming out; or of sons at Eton,Sandhurstor Woolwieh. For instance, there is Lady Hood, whose daughter came out last year, Lady Hothfie'd,whose son is married and in the Guards, Georgina Lady Du iley who is a grandmother, and Lady de Grey who is presenting her daughter—Lady Juliet Lowther—this season. Lady de'Grev was lovely as Lady Gladys Herbert. and afterwards as -Gladys Lady Lansdale, and Lady Juiht—the only child of her first marriage, is almost equally Leautiful, though in so very different a style. Looking at Lady Warwick it seems almost incredible that she can really possess a daughter of fourteen, and a son at Eton, two years older. And it is equally hard to realise that nearly thirteen years have passed since Lady Algernon Lennox appeared at the altar, a lovely bade, Lady Feodore Start, one of the handsomest matrons of the day has been married nearly fourteen years, and Mrs. Carl Meyer longer still. Yet all can bold their own againat the loveliest debutante, and are con- siderably more feted than the girls. Happily, the fashionable woman of ta-day is much more concereel abut her children than was the case ypars ago. She makes a poiut of seeing them more fre- quently, and having them with her as much as possible. In bygone days it was the nurses and governesses who exclusively educa*ed and influenced the little ones. A. glimpse of their mother once a day was all that was ex- pected or looted for. But mothers have been mending in this direction far some time past, and the wiser me- th Ai gains ground year by year. Among the less exalted mothers, too, an improvement has taken p'ace. Instead of sending their children out with young and inexreriencrd nursemaids. whose one aim and ebj 'ct in life seems to be to converse with gen- Vemen in uniform at street earners, they take them walking thernselvea, t hereby benefiting their own health as well as that of tie li.tle folks. They have the chil- dren in tie dining room to me Ile too, much more than fermerly, and ur.dertake the trainiag of their manners at table. All tale means a busy time for the young matron, hut after all it is a gl erious thing to lead a life brimming over with fullness. Sa many lives are meagre, with but a thn thread of purpose and living work running through them. Lt us be thankful to wear out, rather than rust out.

The woman who would keep well in good graces with her men folk, be they brnthere' huiband, father, should tx never he a.ve accepti g their hints as to the dinner menu. An acquaintance of mine when, some two or three year, back, OP became the wife of a man noted among his feeds as a bit of a gourmet; could only prepare and cook the plain- est of dishes. The h )neymooa was a lengthy one how- ever, and inclurled stoppages at a number of hot-Is, *mitts for their cuisine. My friend took careful note of those dishes her husband had a liking for, p,rarl when she had settled down. practised upon them diligently. She was not extrayagart, but she contrived to have al- ways one course that she, knew her hushan I to be fond of. By this means he gradnally became a first class cook, and when on stare occaaicris they wanted to give alittle dinner, it Wa9 always managed quietly and effec- tively. without any nf that fuss and commotion which usually prevsi!s in the kitchen when a dinner party is on the tapir.

For a youthful thruat,a n,chlet of coral beads is quite the favoerite ornamrnt at the mornecti and very be- coming it is. The usual way hal bean to string the beads in several rows, passed through upright slides set with diamonds, hut this method has been improved upon,and roplaeed by another in Which the rays of beads are mounted on a light invisible framework that holds them in position. If diamonds are added, it is in the form of pierced beads, introduced among the 'there. In classifying coal with regard to colour, irrespective of othFr qualities, the dealers distinguish between the red, the black, the clear white and the dull white ; and the red are further subdivided into delp crinecon, pale red, and vermillion, the last: very rare. A delicate rose, or flelh colour is Si seldom t he obtained, and so highly valued, that specimens of this kind are sold at the rats of £lOO to £320 an mine,. The orlinary red coral is only worth about £1 an ounce,and small fra.genents such as are made into children's necklaces cost from le. to 53. an ounce.

We have become so thoroughly accustomeal to chean that an advance in the price thereof will indeed be regarded as a calamity. That advance though, we are assured by those who ought to know,is to come short. It behoves us therefore to look around well, and buy up any short lengths which prlmise to be of use in the creaticn of a blouse,or for a lining or perchance a petti- coat. But we must bear in mind that for the last two purposes the silk mwt be soft, and of the non-rustling persuasion. The woman who rustles now-a-days is lost—from a sartorial point of view. With the bright warm spring wPat,rr, which should shortly come to stay, many of ui will be stowing away our heaviest furs. Great care should be exercised in this operation. First the furs must ho thoroughly beaten, and hung in the sun for at least a couple of hours. Bags of linen must next be, made for each se, and :hese bags should wrap over at each end. ai closely as possible. When filled, they eheuld be deposited in drawers lined with course browla paper which has been previously dampod with turpentine. The edges of this paper must lap over each ethlr more than once, indeed many per- sons will say,the paper should be gummed, and thus, as it were, hermetically sealed. Bitter apple which many. concider good for the purpose in hand I have frequently Wel, with ahsolut?ly no effect in warding off the common house moth. Camphor should never be placed in close proximity to any good fur, as it efftcts the color, while turpentine is always found more successful than anything else. A lengthened sojourn in Russia taught me k him valuable preventative, and tt.e Rwsian furriers' modes operandi is certainly worth knowing. " MADGE."

div.head: TT E EX MTh FE I D I', MARCH 3, 1899.
div.p: TT E EX MTh FE I D I', MARCH 3, 1899.
THE PEACE CRUSADE.
TACKLING THE CONTINENT,
EY W. T. ST'E.A.D.

How is the Crusade of -Peace to be stopped? That may seem an unnecessary and even a foolish question, but it has presented itself seriously to the minds of the organisers. The Crusade has got such a hold of the country that it seems as if the task of bringing it to an end will be far more difficult than that of starting the movement. From snrill teginning the Crusade has gathered force, like an ava!anche sliding down a mountain side, until it is sweeping right through the countri. Almost daily requests for help in the or2anisation tu' meetings right at the end of March are received. Towns which have already had their .big meetings want to !live fresh impetus to the peace movement by other gatherings. On all hands it is apparent that if the head offices were closed to-morrow the. Crusade would run its natural course in ,this c's)untry.

The real struggle will come with the Continent. There has never been any doubt about Engiand. From the very first meetims it has te ri evident that this country is enthusiastically, almost passionately, devoted to peace. That: fact is con- cealed by the newspapers which are supposed by some to reflect public opinion, but nobody who has gone through the experiences which have fallen to my lot during the past two months can retain a doubt on the subject. On the Continent things are very different. We have a: few influential persons workill devotedly for the cause ay.ainst every obstacle that can be placed in their way, but the prolress made is, of course, nothing like that seen in Engsand. If, when the Pilgrims of Peace set out from this country, they are not to plunge into a veritable ice-chamber, all energies must be ,turned to the Continental movement. In the rush and excite- ment of the Crusade in this country, some of us have been a little apt to forget that the original idea was not for a national but an international pilgrimage. England has spoken emphatically and unmistakably. It is for the peace party in Europe to make its voice heard. lam setting out for Paris almost immediately. This will be but a flying visit, for I can only spend one night in France, but I hope to speak at two banquets in the evening, one being that of Americans resident in. Paris. I expect to bring bae.l: an encouraging account of the feeling in Paris, where the work of organisation has been undertaken by M. Passy.. The proper organisation of the Continent cannot be carried out unless money is forthcoming. When this Crusade was started the Finance Cominittee fixed the minimum cost of doing what . has to be done at £lO,OOO. .At least that sum will be wanted, but so far the amount subscribed is less than £3,000. I am not going to beg. It is for those who believe in peace, rich and poor alike, to provide the sinews of the war against war. There are many Men in this country who have made pro- fession of a deep love for peace who could write a cheque for the whole cost of the Crusade without inconvenience. This much is certain. Never has so gigantic a work been undertaken upon so small a sum. Next year, or the year after, it probably be impossible to obtain the same expres- sion of public opinion on an expenditure of £lOO. 000.

From the very first the Crusade has been nobly supported by the leaders of the organised workers in this country. The conference of labour in St. Martin's Town Hall was, in some ways, the most remarkable of London meetings. There was a little opposition, mainly from a small body of Socialists, who wished to move an amendment declaring that peace was impossible until the present politica! order had been changed. But this was admirably managed by the genial chairman, and when the resolution was put it was found that the dis- sentients only numbered five or six. A stirring speech was delivered by Mr. Thomas Burt, and the crowded meeting gave the amplest evidence of the sinceritY of its wish for peace. An outspoken manifesto to the Continental workers was adopted, and Six labcnr leaders were suggested as the repre- sentatives of their class in the pilgrimage.

It will be for the National Convention to choose the Pilgrims of Peace, but it is already apparent that certain men are being marked out by public opinion for the work of carrying the peace gospel on the Continent. A Bishop will certainly be chosen, and among public men it would be a great aid to have Mr. Jolla Morley, Mr. James Bryce, and Mr. Thomas Burt. Some of these, if chosen, would- not be able to go the whole way to St. Petersburg; the claims on their time are too nut emus. But they could all go to Paris, and possibly further, and then the places of these who are compelled to drop out can be filled by others. If, as is now said, the International Conference of the Powers is held about the beginning of May, the Pil-rimae must set out early in April. The best time would pro ally be immediately after Easter, when public men of the calibre of those who must represent this country will have more time to spare.

During the past week as .many as six town's meetings have been held in the course of a singlo night. To attempt to chronicle or to give any account of •thee in the brief space at my disposal is obviously impossible. I have, however, personally attended meetings at Peterborough, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lincoln, Derby, and Oldham. I -had intended to speak also at Southport, but the meeting in that town was postponed by the Mayor. The most successful of the five meetings were those at 'Peterborough, Lincoln and Derby. The large Drill Hall at Peterborough was filled to overflowing with an audience which needed no werning up. From first to last the meeting went w: ii a*,wing. - At Lincoln the best speech of the evening was delivered by the Bishop, who left for a night all controversies about High Church and Low Church, vestments and ceremonies, to speak an emphatic word in favour of the Czar's proposal. The Derby gathering was such as has only been seen in that .town in the midst of the excitement of a General Election. Two thousand persons were present. spoke for an hour and forty minutes, and to the end the huge gathering remained attentive and responsive. The meeting at Oldham was not so good ; the weather was bed, and there were other attractions, which told against a full attendance. On March 21st, a huge meeting is to be held at Queen's Hall in London, at which all the delegates will he invited to attend. The Bishop of London be in the chair, and Mr. ;Tohn Morley has consented to MOTO the first resolution. His speech on the occasion will be eagerly awaited in every quarter of the kingdom. The Marquis of Bristol, who is treasurer of the Crusade, will probably seco-nd the motion. Seats for this meeting will be grit, of all allotted to the delegates appointed by the larions town's meetings all over the country, and we expect to fill the ball with these. If, how- ever, there is any space to spare members of the general public will be admitted. A project is being considered for an afternoon conference as well as the mass meeting in the evening. This night gathering promises to be the most notable held in London for many years past. Men and women representing the whole kingdom, elected by their fellow-citizens as worthy to speak on their behalf, will be gathered into one hall, where every shade of political opinion and almost every religious creed in the. kingdom will have a voice.

div.head: (Copyright.) PRINCESS DELILAH.
div.p: (Copyright.) PRINCESS DELILAH.

BY MRS. GEORGE CORBETT, Author of "When the Sea Gives up its Dead," "The Prince Physician," "The Vindication of Olive Trevethick," "The Star of Yukon," "The Adventures of an Ugly Girl," "Deb o' Many's," "A :Fair Blockade Runner," etc.,

div.head: HAPTER XV.
div.p: HAPTER XV.
DISCREPANCIES.

On the following morning Lord Alfred was up betimes, for he had many inquiries to make, and did not believe in allowing the grass to grow under his feet. He left the house before his sister was downstairs, but he sent a note up to her room, in which be advised her to be as pleasant and affable as possible if Prince Carlos paid her a visit during the day, but on no account to leave the house in conformity with any suggestion or arrange- ment in which he might be concerned. "I have my own reasons," he concluded, "for urging upon you the necessity for extreme caution, and I shall very likely explain myself fully this evening. Meanwhile, it will interest you to know that the object with which I visited Princess Delilah's rooms last night was more than satisfied, and that certain theories which I, had formed were immensely strengthened. Tell the mater not to expect me in to lunch, as I shall be busy all day, and it is just possible that I may call in at the club to dine, instead of coming home until rather late. But above all, do nothing which could give the least idea that my relations with our exalted friends are not of the most cordial description." "If I didn't know that Alfy was one of the most level-headed men in the worrd, " cogitated Lady Flora, after she had read this note, an locked it securely in the pretty davenport which stood in her boudoir, "I should begin to doubt his sanity. For' what strikei, me as no reason whatever, he takes it into his head that there is something wrong with people whose position should place them above reproach. More than that, he asks me to assist him in what he calls his investigations, and I do my best to help him in every respect. I only hope that he isn't starting on a wild - goose chase which will have unpleasant results for him and those whom he is anxious to serve. But no matter how odd his conduct may appear, I know that it is dictated by sound common-sense, so I won't worry him for explanations until he is quite ready to give them. As for Prince Carlos, lam not the least bit in love with him, nor do I appreciate his attentions half as much as I might have done if I had not discovered that he was dividing them with Miss Rizzen-Quicke." ' Lady Flora, it will thus be seen, was a true philosopher, who perpetually tried to make the best of everything, and her brother knew very well that he would be quite safe in giving her even more of his confidence than he had already done. The ionly reason why he did not explain all his con- jectures and plans to her was a desire to protect t her from any evil consequences which might accrue from his interference with the schemes of what he believed to be a daring band of criminals, whose f reputed wealth and station were as powerful to r , avert suspicion from them as they were to afford them opportunities of carrying out their nefarious ;designs. 1 One of the first visitors at Mr. Stree's estab- lishment that morning was Lord Alfred Vavasour- Pomeroy, who was fairly well known there as an occasional customer. In response to his inquiry for Mr. Stree himself, that gentleman soon appeared upon the scene, and Lord Alfred at once entered upon the business which had brought him thither. ... .

4 "I am afraid, Mr. Stree, that I am not likely to prove a very profitable customer this morning,'" he began "for I have simply, come to see if you can enlighten me on one or two subjects." "Ask whatever you like, sir," was the reply, "for I shall be very pleased to be of service to you." "You remember the robbery at the house' of 31y. Rizzen-Quicke, in Piccadilly ? " "Certainly. I took a peculiar interest in that affair, because one of the objects stolen was the Restless Star, a wonderful stone which had narrowly escaped coming into my own hands." "Just so. That particular kind of gem is not very common, is it ? " - "By no means, sir. I have only come across one other in my lifetime. In fact., it is doubtful if more than two of them are known to be in

div.head: existence."
div.p: existence."
"In that case it is somewhat remarkable that you should have dealings in connection with both of them." _ _ .

"Well, it would be, if it were true, my lord. But I think you are slightly mistaken on that point, for although I once had the pleasure of inspecting Restless Star Number Two, the bid I made for it was much below • that of a Russian diamond merchant, who eventually bought it for insertion in the Czar's crown." - - _

t "Then it is not correct that you sold it recently r to the Princess Delilah of Courland ? " "Oh, dear no, sir. The only business I have ever , done with that lady has been to buy from her !several unset diamonds and emeralds which I formerly belonged to her mother, and your linformant niust have unwittingly misled you." "Yes, it is evident that there is some extra- ordinary mistake somewhere. But as you have been courteous in one respect, I am emboldened to ask another favour of you. Can you tell me if there is anything unique or uncommon about this seal ? "

With these words Lord Alfred handed to Mr. Stree the seal which he had found in the Princess Delilah's room, and from which he bad detached the portion of broken chain, and that gentleman examined it with some care.

"Yes," he said presently, "it is so far unique that it is the work of a bygone qeneration. The setting is of a pattern that was very much in vogue twenty or thirty years ago, but which is nowadays considered somewhat too loud for good taste, although it possesses sufficient beauty to make it attractive to anyone who does not follow fashion too closely. The stone is not particularly valuable, although it is a very fine specimen of lapis-lazuli." "Then I may take it for granted that I shall be extremely unlikely to see two or three people wearing a seal exactly of this size and pattern?" "I should say it was very unlikely indeed. But I can quite understand that the owner of this seal would place a somewhat fictitious value upon it, for the stone is neither so rare nor so costly as its beauty would lead inexperienced people to expect." Having gained all the information he came for, Lord Alfred thanked the obliging merchant, and went next to see Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, whom he found engaged in the task of trying to discover among his son's belongings some trace of the destination to which he was proceeding when he last left home. Lord Alfred had not been on peculiarly intimate terms with the vanished Teddy, and when Mr. Rizzen-Quicke asked him to accompany him to the latter's room, it was the first time that he had had the opportunity of observing its interior. A capacious bureau, well-fitted with pigeon-holes, occupied a prominent position near one of the windows, and by way of expediting his search, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke had emptied the whole of the contents into a heap in the centre of the floor. _ _

"I had intended to suggest another careful examination of your son's belongings," said Lord Alfred, after exchanging friendly greetings with the Gold King, "for I • cannot help thinking that we might find something which may be of use in discovering what has become of him. But, mean- while, I have something to shew you. Have you ever seen this seal before ? "
"Why," exclaimed Mr. Rizzen-Quicke in great astonishment, • "that is my own seal, and it belonged to my father before me. Don't you remember me asking Mosenthal how he came by that seal? "

"Yes," was the reply; "that is why I came to you, to verify my belief that I had seen him wearing it." "Well, it's the same article, that's certain. See, here is the very scratch across the face that, is carved on it, which my father pointed out to me. When he gave it to me, he made me promise that I would never part with it, but that I would keep it in memory of him." "But you did part with it?" "Yes, I couldn't help it; and thereby hangs a tale which wouldn'tOnterest you very much. Sammie Mosenthal didn't exactly swindle me out of it, for I daresay the law was on his side. Bit he told plenty of lies over it, and I never was more surprised in my life than when I saw him and it at the Princess Delilah's ball. Afterwards—in fact, it was the very night of the burglary at our house— he called to see me; wanted me to buy a lot of shares in what I considered to be nothing better than a bogus company, and actually offered me my own seal as a bribe. I refused to take his bribe, or to have anything to do with his corn-

pany ; ana it certainly puzzles me to unclemancl how you have come by it now, unless you have got it from Mosenthal himself." °No ; I have not seen Mr. Mosenthal for several days, 'nor have I heard any news concerning him since I saw him last. But I found that seal where nobody else would have looked for it, and I think I know where he spent the evening before his dis- appearance. If we can locate your son at the same place we may safely conclude that we are in a fair way of unravelling the whole mystery." "That is not all I want. If my son is lost to me I mean to avenge him, if it costs every farthing I possess." Mr. Rizzen-Quicke had already made this asser- tion several times, but it had been made in a melancholy, crushed sort of manner, which gave one the impression that, the half-distracted father was hicapable of doing anything himself towards either discovering his son or punishing his presumed abductors. Now, however, the lethargy of grief seemed to leave him suddenly, and he was once more the active, vigorous, clear-headed man of the world, who had raised himself from penury to a giddy pinnacle of fortune. Lord Alfred noticed the favourable change in him, and no longer hesitated to give him his fullest confidence, for there was a chance that he might be able to avoid pitfalls into which he might other- wise stumble, unless he knew how essential it was to be on his guard against Prince Carlos and his friends.

' "You believe that those people are at the bottom of the mischief I " he exclaimed, after his first incredulous astonishment had disappeared. "And I have been encouraging their visits, when I ought to have kicked them out of the house!" "Hush!" was Lord Alfred's caution. "Yon must not, do anything rash, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, and you must encourage their visits more than ever for a few days, until we have discovered to what extent our suspicions are correct. Only don't let the Duke hypnotise you again. Remember that there is always safety in numbers, and that he is not likely to exercise his fatal power except when alone with his intended victim."

"Well, I don't know. It really seems too wild for belief • and yet, the more one thinks of it, the more likely does it seem that you are right; for when I heard that sham detective's voice, it seemed a bit familiar to me; and whoever the fellow was, he must have gleaned some information about my habits, or that cheque business would not have been managed quite so easily. As for the burglary, this theory would help to confirm your idea that it was at first. merelY intended to make it appear that the star sapphire was stolen that night, and that the theft of emeralds and diamonds was simply a sequel to the original plan. I wonder if any of my people were mixed up in it ? " To this conjecture Lord Alfred offered no verbal comment, but shewed himself exceedingly interested in a fragment of blotting-paper which he had rescued from the heap on the floor. Holding it in front of the dressing-glass, he looked critically at the reflection of some words which were impressed on, RI and managed to decipher a few of them:

"Your commlids . : . prove . . . . goddess shall have . . re your promise „ . . devoted . . ." Disconnected and unsatisfactory as this scrap of information was, Lord Alfred felt that it was really of great importances; for he gathered from it inferentially that Teddy Quicke had undertaken to procure something valuable at the command of a lady with whom he was wildly in love. It had been well known that he was in this state with reference to the Princess Delilah; and there was no necessity to strain the imagination very much to arrive at the conclusion that the star sapphire was the object she coveted. Legally, it might prove very difficult to convince others that Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke's star sapphire was not reposing snugly in her jewel case until after the Princess Delilah had been seen wearing the one which she was supposed to have bought lately. Morally, Lord Alfred had not the slightest doubt on the subject;, and he grimly resolved that if the modern Delilah was really using her beauty to entrap men to their ruin, her career as an honoured member of London society should not last much longer. "There does not seem to be anything else here," remarked Lord Alfred to Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, "which will throw, any light upon your son's dis.. appearance. But I fancy this bit of blotting-paper will go a long way; and, since I came here, another thought has occurred to me. Do you think that Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke would be able to recognise the diamonds and emeralds which have been stolen from ber ? "

"She would, if they are still in the same con- dition in which they were stolen. And so would I, for that matter, for I bought the two necklaces myself; and you'll not find many finer ones in a long day's walk." • "Of course, the necklaces would be easily recog- nised; and equally, of course, it is not at all likely that,you will see the diamonds and emeralds in the form of necklaces again. But it will be much more important to think of the gems quite apart from their setting; and, at any rate, you will have formed a rough estimate of their size and number ? " "My wife is very methodical, and she keeps a coniplete list of all her jewellery, together with an elaborate description of each item." "Then I must ask you to do me a favour. Will you and Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke accompany me at once to the establishment, of Mr. Stree, who has recently bought froni a lady of exalted station several unset diamonds and emeralds of unusual magnificence ? "
CHAPTER XVI. Cc HAVE YOU HEARD OF MADAME _CELIA ? "

It was necessary to display a certain amount of tact in inspecting the diamonds and emeralds which Mr. Stree had recently bought from the Princess Delilah, for Lord Alfred's investigations had not proceeded so far that he felt justified in shewing his suspicions openly • and it was as intending purchasers that Mr. and Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke pre- sented themselves, though their hearts were too heavy for them to take the slightest pleasure in their ostensible errand.

Contrary to expectxtion,. there appeared to be no grounds for supposing that these were the identical gems of which Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke had been deprived. Those had been in graduated sizes, with large stones in the middle of the neck- lace, and smaller ones towards the back; whereas these were of almost uniform size, every one of them being equal to the finest she had possessed. Several important purchases were made by way of indemnifying the merchant for his courtesy; but it was felt that the errand had been a failure, and ?Ar. and Mrs. Quicke went home somewhat de- jectedly, after being earnestly cautioned against showing themselves either too suspicious or too careless when dealing with Prince Carlos and the Duke of Hapsburg-Solltesein. Lord Alfred was not so easily daunted, for he had not such heart-wearing grief to contend against as was the case with the vanished Teddy's father and mother; and he occupied the rest of the morning in paying a visit to Mr. Raleigh, whom he luckily found disengaged. On comparing notes, it transpired that even the authorities had discovered very little more than was already known concerning the disappearance of Mr. Sammie Mosenthal, except that he had so manipu- lated all the money which had been paid for shares in the Electrolytic Goldmakers' Company that not one of the shareholders was likely to see any of it again. In short, the business was a colossal fraud; and there were few people to be found who did not believe that Mr. Mosenthal was simuly an absconding swindler, about whose disappearance there was nothing more tragic than is usual in such cases.

"Things certainly look black against Mosenthal," agreed Lord Alfred. "But even if he was willing to dupe the investors, it must still be granted that the incident of the broken watch-chain is a suspicious one; and there can be no accusation of trubezzlement brought against either Mr. John or Mr. Edward Rizzen-Quicke." Mx. Raleigh had a great respect for people in iiigh places, and Lord Alfred Vavasour-Pomeroy's investigations seemed to him to be trending more towards mental hallucination than towards a successful unravelling of an ominous mystery: yet he was careful to agree with him on every point— or it was not possible to pick up a profitable client every day—and in the event of Lord Alfred's theories not being quite so mad as they seemed, there was at least the chance of some share of glorification accruing to Mr. Raleigh himself. He, therefore, worked very diligently on the lines sug- gested by his client, and he had already done the latter a valuable service.

"Yes, my lord," he said, in answer to an inquiry, "I have discovered the residence of the lady you wish to see, and have made an appointment for this evening at nine o'clock, on the understanding that if it is inconvenient for you to attend then, you will go to-morrow at the same time." "Business like this does not permit dalliance," was Lord Alfred's decisive reply. "I will go to- night, and if Madame Celia's powers are as wonderful as I have been led to believe, I may Snake some imuortant discoveries."

The time and place of meeting with the detective being agreed upon, Lord Alfred felt that it behoved him to attend to his own needs; and he was very much invigorated after lunchin_q, and restinc,, at his club. Four o'clock in the afternoon found him in Polly Rizzen-Quicke's society; and he improved his opportunities to• such purpose that the tack engagement which already existed between them developed into a formal one, it being fully under- stood between the lovers that they would not marry until it had been discovered what had become of Teddy. "And, do you know," observed Polly, "I have got a curious fancy to-day? My maid has behaved very strangely ever since the burglary. She says that she was so frightened at the idea of burglars coming into the house that she cannot sleep at nights, for fear of waking up and finding a`,burglar in her room. I can quite understand her nervous- ness, but it seems to me that she carries it a little too far, and it wouldn't surprise me to discover that she knows% more about that night's transactions than she cares to tell." _ _

This was an interesting suggestion to Lord Alfred, for it lent colour to his own suspicion that someone indoors had been suborned ,by the burglars to make everything smooth for them. "I must have a watch set on your maid," he remarked, after a little further conversation with Polly. "What is her name ? " "Alice—Alice Johnston." _

"Very well. Alice Johnston will for a little while be too well watched to play you any more tricks. It is quite possible that she is a good girl, whose conscience is pricking her for a complicity which she could no more help than your father could help doing what the sham detective told him to do." "Good gracious! Do you mean to say that she has been hypnotised too? " "That remains to be proved. If My supposition is correct, there is probably a pretended lover in the case, whom Alice must have met frequently, though it by no means follows that the acquaint- ance is being kept up, now that the burglary is an accomplished fact, and even the strictest watch upon the girl may fail to be of assistance to us. Still, one never knows, and we cannot afford to neglect the slightest chance of solving the mysteries which surround us." _ _

I "But, Alfred," remonstrated Polly, "it seems too preposterous to believe that the Duke of Hapsburg-Solltesein would pose as the lover of a lady ' s-maid 1" "Aid why not? If he is the all-round scoundrel I believe him to be, he will stand at nothing which will further his plans. By the bye, had be or the Prince anything of importance to say last night when they were here ? ' "Yes. What they had to say was very important in their estimation, for the Prince came to urge his suit once more, and his fidus Achates accompanied him, no doubt intending to influence my mother to insist upon my acceptance of the honour offered me. But the mater had a terrific headache, and 'couldn't leave her room, and father and I were some sort of protection for each other. A few minutes after they came, we had two or three other visitors, whose presence effectually put an end to confidential talk of any description. So the Duke and the Prince speedily departed again, and I have .not seen them since. But here comes mother, look- ing very much upset. I wonder what can be the matter with her ? " _ _

Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke, who entered the room at this moment, really did ,look very much disturbed, and explained that her agitation was caused by the Duke of Hapsburg-Solltesein and the Prince of Mitylene. "They called a little while ago," she said, "and I would have asked them into the drawing-room, if your father had not been with me, although I am beginning to distrust them both. But your father interfered, and sent word down by Clayton that we were none of us at home. If there's any spook business about that Duke,' he said, I want us to see no more of him than we can help, for we can't afford to let either him or anybody else send our wits woolgathering again; and if we can't get hold of any better Dukes and Princes than these are, we'll be content with knowing honest men who haven't a title to bamboozle us with.'" I "Then am I to consider myself banished ? " inquired Lord Alfred, with a slight smile which materially increased Mrs. Bizzen-Quicke's perturba- tion. "Or is my title too insignificant to bring ma into disrepute? ' "Oh, dear no, my lord!". was the confused reply. "Pray don't think that he was alluding to you, for both he and I have tho:!, greatest respect for yon."

These words paved the' way for the request Lord Alfred had to make, and, in spite of a curious impulse which induced Mrs. Rizzen-Quicke to bring forward the objection that Polly was practically pledged to the Prince of Mitylene, he soon won her consent to his engagement. Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, who followed his wife to the drawing-room as soon as he had assured himself that the people whose bona fides he had begun to doubt had really taken their departure again, was unaffectedly delighted to hear that Polly had accepted a suitor whose mental and moral qualifications were quite on a par with his social ones. "Of course I'll have you for a son-in-law," he said cordially. "Jane has been holding out for the Prince of Mitylene, but I think I've convinced her that he isn't to be trusted; and, anyhow, we've something besides ambition to think about. Why, I'remember--" What Mr. Quicke remembered just then was kept for future disclosures for his wife suddenly required his presence elsewhere, and the rest of the afternoon was spent by the lovers in planning the beautiful , life they were to lead after Teddy had been found. Then Lord Alfred was asked to stay to dinner, and accepted the invitation, but excused himself soon after he had dined on account of an important Appointment he had to keep. d'And," he concluded, "I am not sure that you wouldn't like to come with me, Mr. Rizzen-Quicke, for I hope to make great discoveries to-night. 'Rave you heard of Madame Celia, the clairvoyante ? " "I don't know whether father has, but I have," interjected Polly. "They say that she does the most extraordinary things; that she can tell all about your past, and that you have only to put an article into her hand while she is in the clairvoyant state for her to be able t 9 describe various scenes in which the owners of the articles have participated." "That is exactly what i have heard," observed Lord Alfred, "and I intend to test her powers to-night. If all that is said about her is true, a certain piece of blotting-paper, which bears the im— pression of Mr. Edward Rizzen-Quicke's writing, will bring us news of him; and a certain seal N5-ill enlighten us concerning the fate of Mr. Mosenthal.*

WYCLIFFE P.S.A. SOCIEPY.-OPEN..MEETING:

iti;;l;e7a-r&itir-ig—being an open one for both sexes, there was a large atteadance.Mr. S. B.Stringer presided, and in the course of a brief address he deprecated the habit of criticism and sensorious judgment of persons by parents in the heariog of their children. He referred to cases where it had had injurioue resulte—efr. Chandos Wilson, of Minchester,was the speaker for the afternoon, and spoke upon what the P.S.A. Soeiety was trying to do. He said he understood it was trying to help men to live lives that were jciet, true, upright, forbeariae, patient and kind; lives meat would be a blessing to them and a boon to all with whem they came in contact. If he understood it aright the P.S.A. movem.nt was seek- ing through the hearts and lives of its members, par- ticularly through the jives of its numbers, to make earth a little more like heaven. Thie speaker proceeied by means of a story to drive home to his hearer e several useful lessons.—A trio party consisting of Miss Christian, Miss Harrop and Miss Bothwell sane a couple of trios in an efficient manner.—Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. pre- sided at the organ.—['tie Rev. John Yorige stated that; on the following Sunday the society would commence its seventh year. When the society commenced th,re were people who prophesied that it would live for six months, and after that period elapsed they said they would know no more about it. They had now completed six years and he hoped there would be a large re-enrol- ment for the next year. It was only fair to state that the number of members during the past year was not quite so large as during the previous twelve mouths, the numbers having fallen from 905 •to 770. There were reasons for that diminution of members. The P.S.A. movement was not quite 83 new as it was, and several men's classes had been started which had been drawing some of their members away. There was no reason to complain or grumble about that. If they had done good by their meetings and other churches— not excepting the Established Church—had taken a leaf out of their book by starting men's meetings, there was reason for thankfulness and courage ler the future.—The service was also taken part in by Mr. John Atkinson and Mr. Thomas Hawthorn. THE DEATH AND RESURRECTION OF CHRIST. Mr. E. Bellamy. of Stockport, lectured in the Christa- delphian Room, Bold-street, on Sunday night, his subject being " The love and power of God, manifest in the Death and Rearrrection of Christ."—The Lecturer statee that beforethey could understand the love of God as manifested in the death of Christ they must understand the things concerning their own nature. If they believed in the pagan doctrine of immortal soulism ; of heaven going at death ; or the waning idea of Heli going, it was impeisible for them to realize how GA's love and power were thus manifested. " dod only hare immortality," and on referring to the Ist Corinthiara 15 they:would see that this mortal was to put on learner- talityethis corruptible was to put on incorruption. They were enjoined to seek for immortality but if they already had an immortal soul what was the goad of seeking for something which they possessed. Examining the record of maws creation, Mr. Bellamy pointed out the fact that the word soul was applied equally to lower animals,birds and that Adam became a living soul—act a never dying soul. Put under a law which he trans• greased, his sentence was death—dying thou shalt die— and the malty and curse thus introduced no peace society could take away but 'Christ would remove it shortly. The sentence affected each one present (Romacns-12) but if they were made like Christ death would have no more dominion over them. They would be made like Chris; if they were in Christ. and continued walking faithfully. They could be in Christ by the means which God had appointed pnd no other. They must know Christ if they were to believe him and they could know him from the Bible alone. The thine written in the law of Moses and in the prophets and in the psalms concerning him must net be ignored as they could not put on Christ. They were heirs or not heirs according to the promise and they could determine their position by Galatians 30, 27-29. The earth was promised to Christ and if they accepted God's condition they also might have an inheritance in the good time coming. "CUBIST AND SOCIAL ORDER: THE GOAL BEFORE 13S:" _

On Sunday afternoon- -at--St.-J-aertes'Church, the Rev. F. E. Powell, delivered an address on the abeve subject. In the course or hie remarks, the rev. gentleman said as they surveyed human life they were inevitably led to form one of two cencluiions, either that there was a fatherly will at the base of all things or there was not. It there was not then, with Mr. Balfour. " the very exis- tence of man on this earth is an accident,his history but a brief and transitory episode in the life of one of the meanest of the planets," and nothing would eventually be the better or the worse for all that had been. As they looked upon human life there was indeed much to make them lose heart and give way to despair. There was, for instance, the continued menace of war, twenty millions of men ready to redlen earth's fields with bleoi Seven-eighths of the people,too,belonged to a class whose average income was to say the least miser tbly inade- quate, and multitudes with ineufficient food and cloth- ing for the maintenance of a healthy life. But in spite of these tremendous temptations to pessimism they had in the revelation of the Bible, and esp-cially in the Christ, something to busby them up and te support their faith. Young ardent souls, cnnscious of the wrong in society, rushed forth with their utopian ideals to put things right. Their ideals were, however, apt to be quenched as they contemplatei, not only the real, but the indifference which too often accompanied the real. Well, the mistake such made was in thinking they were to mould and re form society in their own way, in accordance with their orn ideal. What they had to do was to be conscioas that anther Mealder was at work. God had been educating the race from its infancy until now, by the experience of toil and sorrow, by the anguish of sin and death,by the failures and disappointments of life their ideals were not always fulfil;ei. They were conscious of unretche I aims, imexpresiee thoughts, unsatiated throbbings of desire. But let them cousole themselves with the reflection that there was a social order towards which they were moving. and that this social order was not man's, but God's. He was the great Evolver. Let them then look for Ilk ideal, sni work for that far-off Divine event to whch the whole creation moved. That faith cave a bre telth and a dig- nity to the view of man's destiny, and immeaeurably enlarged the significence of human life. If God's great Social Order depended upon it the perfection of the in- dividual and the perfection of human society would he accomplished. In the century new clesine there had been great physical changes, in that now coming there would be equally great political and social changes. And SO the destiny of human life would work itself ou'.Each change was preparing for the final goal--Lhe estab:ish- merit hero on earth of that New Jerusalem, teat new heaven and new earth wherein develleth rightenusnesa or justice, or that perfect Social Order wherein God's will would be done in earth as it is in heaven THE REV. W. IC DRUMMOND ON RITUALISM

AND TEIE RITUAL CONTROVERSY. At Cairo-street Chapel on Suaday evening, the Rev. W. H. Drummond spoke upoa"Ritualism and the Rirmal Controversy." He took as his text "They that worship Me must worship Me in spirit and in truth." At the outset he pointed out that the subject he wished to speak about was one which was causine a keen con- troversy. Lie did not speak in tha spirit of a ptrtisan, but rather in the spirit of the great prayer of Christian charity. Da not let them approach the subject in a spirit of bitterness or of unreasnna.ble antagonism. Let them try to understand how religious rit ial came to ex- ist. It was the outward ex.pretsion of religious feAinz and worship. Ritual was simply the langua.7o n r?liaion when nun gatbrred together, not for practical god works, but for the worship of GA. Man was both soul and body ;be loved material coniitions and eves his wor- ship when most spiritual could not lie Srnara.vd from outward and visible form.. Thee could not du without forms in their re igion. The g,e It question was what were the for:na to tv., but as soon al they had asked that qufstion the 7 brcime aware that there was a strong divergence of opinion am3ng men. There was on the one hand the tendency to kay grea.t stress upon outward f >rms, and on the other hand there were others wha trok the Puritan view, and whilst acknowlrdeing that they must have outward t)rals in religioa they were

desirous that they should be as simple as possible. They felt that all forms of this kind seernei to come between the soul and Go.l and theref ma they must be kept down as much as possible. Tnese two types had ofteh bean unfair to each other. Many of them who hid Noncon- formst and Puritan blood in their veins perhaps found it somewhat difficult t be quite fair to in.ln who felt in regard to these matters very differeatly from themselves. Tnere had been In their tim s a great revival for outward forms and a great development of religious ritual. They had a powerful and growing ritualistic party in the religious life of the country 'which had given rise to a certain amount of se re 'ain z of heart amongst thsse who believed that these beautiful religious forms were in great danger of sinhing into formalism. They could net doubt that there were mans' men at the present time who were laying great stress upou ritual, svhese services were crowded by large con- gregations who all the time were the victims of an un- rest religion. Thy had no deep spiritual convic-Aons in their minds to correspond with the outward ritual which was so vital. Ile should,be the last .to charge any class of men as a whole with religious insincerity. He knew full well that the mast active and the must earnest of the men in the ritualistic party were not insincere. Tee preacher then proceed •d to state his objections to ritual- ism. In the first place he said the ritualistic view of religion and tile great stress laid upon the sacraments and upon speeial sacred places and seasons made reigion so material. It seemed to take the grace of Gid and confine iE to ceNain prescribed material channels. Their experience of religion 'and Chrietian truth contradicted this narrow and m tterial view. It *as contrary to the very spirit and temper of tee whole of the New Testament teaching. In tne sec and plan this belief of Goi which corresponded to on: ward ritual, and which this ritual was the language and expreszion of was a medieval and not a modern plaice. It took us back to a bygone age and to men whose view of the world was narrow and limited, and whose view of God's love Was more confined than taeirs of ths present day. They could not go back for the foo I of their souls to men whose thoughts of God were narrow and material. Toe preacher then proceeded to refer to what the effect of ritualism WhE3 likely to have upon character, and upon the national life. He felt that it tended to slacken their hold upon the great principles of righteousness,and that the men influenced by ritualism would htve less back- bone than those whose religion bad been founded for so long upon the imperishable rock of the righteouesess of God.
ST. ANN'S CHURCIa —TFIIRTIETH ANNIVERSARY
OF CONSECRATION.

The 30th anniversary of tee consecration of St. Ann's Church was celebrated on Sunday by spcial services. The sermon in the morning was preached by the Rev. P. J. Byrne, audio the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Vicar (the Rev. J. Davies). Cellectioes were taken on beholf of the augmentation fund.—On 11onday evening a service was held, And the Rev. Dr. Porter, of Southport, preached. Taking for his text "Fear, not little dock; for it is your Father's good pleasure te give you the kingdom" (St. Luke xii. 32), he said that the emotion of tear was created by sin, and if they made themselves worthy of the Lo:APs inyitatioa they need have no dread in the present or of the future. Ia C3ll- - his discourse he said that for 39 years the gospel had been preached in that church. Wisat a blessed thing it was that all over the land, in the big to'. us and in the little villages and country pla::es,there were calcturaries in which the everlasting gospel was being preached ! What a mighty work had been dme threughout the country, and yet some men were trying to get back to the nensense of Rome, to introduce into their Church the whole of the paraphernalia of Rome. _Spain to-day was a standing example of the tutsery.vice, and poverty Rome could bring about. Tnere was there one priest to every few hundreds of the population, ald about seven in every ten people could neither read nor write. Would they like to see such degradation in England? The English Church had given forth the Word of Life, not only in this country, but to the ends of the world, and where the Union Jack flew there also was the everlastine gospel.—A. collection was taken in aid of the workers fund.

RUGBY FOOrBA.LL. The result of Saturday's match was not an unexpected one, for it could hardly be expected that Warrington would prove anything like a match for Broughton Rangers, the leaders of the competition. Optimists fancied that there was a chance, seeing the poor display made by the Rangers against Tyldesley, but the hops was indeed a vain one. Warrington were well beaten as the score of 19 points to 2 shows conclusively. The scoring m trgin was a mach greater one than I expected for Warrington are generally able to give the Rangers a tight game, but on Stturiay they found their opponents in tip top foran and suffered accordingly.

Broughton Rangors, though the season is so far ad- vanced,have not done with importing.On Saturday they tried a new forward, a sprightly chicken of 14 stones weight, who is already plssessed of international honours. It is Warrington's luck to have these new in. ternationals tested against them. Oldham to3k advan- taze of their visit to Warrington to test the mettle of Torn D avies,tbe best centre tnreequarter they have got. Blth these men signalised the event by scoring a try. The Rangers' new forward is one Joe Blacklock, late of Aspatria, a player of magnificent physique. It makes one sigh with envy tn see so many such men in one team. Brouzhton have an exceptionally powerful front rank whic'i will be further strengthened by the inclusion of such a giant as Blacklock.

Thouo the great game between Salford and Swinton was taking place only a few miles away there was a goodly crowd to welcome Warringtoaat Wheaters' Field. I winning team can always command support,and there wer3 fully 6,000 people round the Rangers enclosure. The lat:er compares unfavourably with the playing patch at Wilderspool. Grass does not thrive in tae neighbour- hood of Manchester and the time has yet to C 31119 when I shall see it on Wheater's Field. Why, even poor, slan- dered. oleriferaus Widnes can show greener turf than Broughton. The ground was not in bad condition for football, however.

OF course one never expects Warrington to do much when they go away from la)ms withaut their captairs, but Bate's absence had not m ich ta da with the result of Saturday's game. It was not at half-back where Warrington compared unfavourably with their oppon- ents but at three-quarters and full blck. In other de- partmghts of the game they quite held their own and on several occasions had hard luck in f Ailiag ta scare.

Play up to the interval was of rather a surprising character. For the first (part r-of-ae-hour the visitors played a style of foo'LMall which would have won them the game had it been maintained. The forwards' heeled oat rapidly and the backs combined with an effectiveness which kept the Rangers busy defeadiug. Several passing runs by the Warrinton men were worthy of more famous teams. Then a change came o'er the scene. Hallam wade tvoured to do more than his duty called for hire to do, anel failing to elude the home forwards be was tackled near his own tine. Tile burly Rangers used their a 'vantage te some purpose, and were not long in crediting themselves with points. A long pass to 10 the lengthy Jackson" resulted in this player scoring a splßnd.d try, though several attempts were made to stop him. Warrine,zon were momentarily demoralised, and as is often the case, before they coull pull themselves to- gether another try had bell registered, Barratt being the scorer. 'Twas not long ere Sam Jams added a third, and Chapman a goal. By this time,—too late of course—Warrington had got their second wind, and paying a visit to the opposite end were re warded with a goal.

The teams had an equal share of the gams in the second half, but the R augers did all the scoring. Black- lock opened the slcoud account with a try whicn it was little us' anytrdy trying to prevent. When such a man as he takes it into his head to rush the line from short range, it is practically hopeless for backs of the size ef vVatrington's to attempt to check his progress. I had a fleeting vision of one or two players coming near the scorer, but I fancy the wind raised by his headlong passage through the air swept them out of the way. Something di 1 at all events, and the 196t05. weight was allowed to lie on the inoffandiug oval. It was a cruel shame, but that did not prevent Chapman kicking another goal. Finally Jarkson get in f it the second time after 133ing once repulsed and almost held. Warring- ton's only consolation as that the score fell short of twenty points and they were not willed.

On the winning side the most dangerous man was un- doubtedly Jsckson.His great speed and strength enabled hinn t score both his tries on occasions when an ordin- ary wing player would:have had no opening whatever. In addition he bottled Harris up completely, and the dash- ing Warrington player had few opportunities of escaping the vi,zila..ine of his big adversary. Barratt aad Chap- man played a fine cmtre game.and were continually put in posseision of the ball by the two James's who played clever,sc entitle football all tarough.Dansoa was poor on the rizht wing. On the home side Hallam compared unfavourably with nis vis-a-vis, Da.*, and played by far itie wort game he has ev.r played since he filled BDICOP7'3 place. He was tackled repeatedly, and fielded the bill badly. Fish played a consistently uod game, while Isherwood and Wood were about on a par. Wood showed considerable improvement, but will have to smarten up a lot if he is to be of much servieeto the club. The most prominent and useful man on the Warrington side was Mice's. who played a splendid game at half- back and is proving himself a god capture. S Mlle of the openings he made on Saturday were worthy of the absent "Smack" himself. kshurst was also in fine form, and at half back and forward the team renthred a good accoont of itself.

Widnes accomplished a splendid pnformince by de- feating the all-conquering Oldham team. though toe margin was only 2 points. They played a killing game, and with such a tower of strength behind as flit,y th bottled their clever opoonents up completely. Oldnam had decidedly the worst of it. The visit of Broughton Ringers to the SIMI ground to-lay will be a tit-bit, and if they too fall victims to Widnes rushes them the e.hampionship will be in an interesting state. Broughton's forwards ought to stud then in good stead, but they will be lucky if they do better than Oldham managed to d 1.

At noon, on Tuesday, Sir Herbert Croft made his annual inspection of the Warrington p slice. The men paraded at the Drill Hall under the command of the Chief Constable (Mx. Luke Talbot). There were on parade Superintendent Monaghan and four members of the detective staff; Inspectors Phillips, Rowbotham, and Taylor, Sergeants Evans, Flolling- worth, Williamson, Lewis, Chantler, Dean and Bell, and 40 con-tables. The strength of the force is now a men. After an examination of the clothing, &c., and the usual inquiry as to complaints, the men were put through a number of drills by Inspector Phillips. The inspe3tion was witnessed by the Mayor, the Deputy Mayor, Councillor Rogers and Heaton, Mr. G. F. F. White (d-Tuty magistrates' clerk), and Dr. R. Smith (police surgeon). Upon the dismissal of the man, Sir Herbert Croft, accom- panied by the Chief Constable and Superintendent Monaghan, proceeded to the Police Station, where the cells, offices, and books were inspected. At a meeting of the Council of the Chamber of Commerce held at Market Gate Chambers, on Mon- day, the president (Alderman Roberts) in the chair, the following new members were elected :—Messrs. Richard Evans and Company, Limited, Messrs. Henry Milling and Company, Limited and 11Ir. J B. Isaac —The president, vice-president, secretary, and other members who could make it convenient to at- tend were appointed delegates to the annual meet- ing of the Associated Chambers of Commerce, to be held in London on March 14th. 15th, and 16th. The programme, which was of a very interesting charac- ter, was considered, and instructions were given to the delegates with reference to several of the more important items.—The Secretary reported that he had not yet received any further information from the Ship Canal Company, with reference to the facilities afforded by the lay-by for local traffic, but he believed that the lay-by had not yet been used, and that it was most desirable that steps should be taken to render it available for heal traffic.—The Secretary was requested to communicate with the Ship Canal Company further upon the subject, and to ask them for cer ain details with reference to the charges, &c.—A. communication was read from Mr. H. 11. Niarks, concerning alleged deficiencies in British Consular Service as computed with that of the United States, and a number of suggestions were made with a view to imuroving the same, the general opinion being that, British manufacturers wer3 unduly handicapped as the result of the de- fects complained of.

Members of both sexes attended in large num- bers the last meeting held by Ntr. A. E. Windle in the Parr Hall on Sunday evening. There was no chairman on this occasion as Mr. Windle conducted the whole proceedings himself, and these proceed- ings were totally different to those of the previous gatherings. The former subjects had reference solely to t`te physical aspects of man but on Snnday evening Mr. Windle took a new departure and dealt exclusively with the spiritual needs of mankind. After the opening exercises the Y.M.C.A. secretary read as his lesson the 40th Psalm, and subsequently based his address upan the 2nd verse of the same chapter. The address really consisted of a chapter of autobiography which was listened to with in- tense interest throughout its narration. The point of the addresa was the hepeless spiritual condition in which the speaker found himself, even after baptism and episcopal confirmation. He vividly described his realisation of the tact that, notwith- standing all the outward religious observances and rites to which he had sincerely sub mitted,he was a confirmed sinner, and he grephic illy allude i to the "Slough of Despond " in which, for twelve weary moats, he groped his way. _ After that time he gradually succeeded in gaining the edge of the "Slough "and eventually by the assistance of the Rev. Thos Waugh, WeFlayan evangelist, he earns within sight of the joys of the " Celest'al City." In conclusion he related how he came into full pessessi of the happiness anl pace of heavenly citizenship and made a powerful appeal to his hearers to leave theuhorrible pit" of sin and to enter into the spiritual light which he enjoyed —lie asked those who were desirous of amending their present mole of life to signify the same by uplifting their rightlands, and seeing the taro response he requested tho4e woo felt in need of sairitual salvation to make their way into the ant e.r.)om. S) large was the resumse to this invitation that the room was hardly large enough to contain the enquire!s and the WICKOri, the latter beine simply overweeleted by the magnitude of the work Having by this tine s concluded the meeting Mr. Winile came and ad tressed the seekere after light, and most of them, if not all, de- clared that whereas they were once blind, they had now received eighr.—Ou Monday evening a number of the converts met in the SiCtetxrv's office at the Y.M.C.A. and from Messrs. A. E Whiffle, John S Green, E T Lei.gh and It J Moss, received further instruction relative to the Caristien life.

Seton-Karr, the brother of the Comer. va.tive member for Sr. Helens, has sent Dr. Lunn some interesting details of his lion hunting expedi- tion to Somaliland. He writes tinier the date of January 8-,h as follows:- "You will be glad to hear that yesterday Sir Edmund Lech mere killed a fine lion in the open. Lady Lech mere was close to her husband and they were both on foot. The distance from the lion was 23 yar is. I reserved my fire in case of the lioa charging. Lady Lechmere is a, second Lady Baker. We were all very 'done ' hav- ing followe I the lion's tracks at a fast rate frosS 10 30 a.m. till 2-35 p m , when we suddenly came on it. We might have hid ta follow farther, only luckily it ha i kided a fine oryx beisa (a large ante- lope allied to the gemsbak of ',lashrnaland) and was lying by it. We had heard the lion routing its the early hours of the morning. The other two members of our p arty hal killed a lion, and two bon4 and a rhinokteros resipctively ten days ago, probably others by now. Tne 111911 gave us three Eagliih cheers when we got to camp. The climate is delictoaa, but we are all very sunburnt. *the caravans are working splendidly, but we have lost some camels.
