WE do not know how the
A Constitutional

Question. English Church Union could expect any other reception than that which has been given to their manifesto of revolt and defiance. Nearly all the leading journals take the same view of the terms and de- clarations that document contains. They are grave, critical, and lawless. They raise a constitu- tional question of the very first importance, upon which in the country at large there can be only one opinion. We have used the term lawlessness in the general controversy about Ritualism, and we can now add to it, as the " Times " does, the word "anarchy." The Union denies that the Crown and Parliament have any rights in deter- mining questions of doctrine, discipline, and cere- monial, and the denial makes the whole question one in which every loyal person, whatever his or her religion may be, has a constitutional voice. The supremacy of the Crown and of Parliament is impeached. These Dissenters within the Church are as bad as the anarchists who make war on the State. If there be any thing more fixed and more unassail- able than another it is the supremacy of the Crown and of Parliament. There can be no security for free4lom, equality, and peace unless this constitu- tional doctrine, laid down in all our text boeks, accepted by all our courts, and by politicians and religionists of all denominations, is put beyond question. Parliament cannot admit the existence of any body in the country which denies its rights. There is no cther body which presumes to make the denial. It is an impudent, offensive, and illegal declaration. It will make the present crisis more acute, deepen the character of the ecclesiasti- cal difficulty, and it will compel prosecutions which it was hoped might be avoided. The Church, which is called national, cannot be allowed to claim or exercise powers superior to the State, the tribunals it appoints, the Bishops it selects, the Articles it has approved, the faith which is established by law. We have now to deal with a political and constitutional question, upon which there cannot be nnich room for any large difference of opinion. If the members of the English Church Union will not submit to the de- cisions of the tribunals which the State has set up, rebellion will have to be punished. There is no alternative for the country, which cannot admit an imperium in imperio without endangering its own existence. The persons who place themselves above the law and outside the legiblative control of Parliament and the headship of the Sovereign are rebels. Their logical course of conduct is to secede at once, and to join the Roman Catholic communion, while liberty of doctrine, discipline, and ceremonial is unknown. There is no cause for alarm except as to the unity and peace of the Church. The State will assert and protect itself against schismatics and perverters of doctrine, even if it has to embark on a struggle more severe than this coun ry has suffered since the Reformation. Law and Protestantism, Parliament and Episcopacy, are defied. It may be only a penny-trumpet defiance, but it will arouse the country; and we are entering upon a struggle which must either end in ejection or secession.
No one can be satisfied with A Troubled the general outlook. Never Outlook.

in our time have there been so many outstanding difficulties in the world at large. Probably Holland and Switzerland are the only two Powers which can regard the outlook with satisfaction. Sweden and Norway do not seem to have quite composed their international troubles. Denmark has bitter feelings against Germany for expelling Danes from Schleswig !Holstein, and Belgium has grave disturbances to encounter in the Congo. Spain has suffered a great humiliation, and Portugal is on the verge of bankruptcy, and nervously awaits the arbitration respecting Delagoa Bay. The condition of Russia's foreign policy i 3 not free from anxieties. The railway questions in China threaten to further- involve her in trouble with thi9 country. Austria looks with apprehen- sion to the turmoil in Bosnia and a possible out- break in Macedonia, whilst the Hungarian diffi- culty is but temporarily patched up. Turkey is expecting to be disturbed by Servia and Bulgaria, and has already something like chronic rebellion to deal with in Yemen. Italy has the conference trouble, and a fateful decision immediately ahead as to the Triple Alliance. Germany has come to a secret agreement with this country as to certain eventualities in Africa and probably in China aliiout the massacre of German subjects. France is pass- ing through a period of storms and stress at home and abroad. The United States, which have been so long exempt from the responsibilities of empire have entered upon a policy which is likely to give tkem new problems to solve and to entail a heavy expenditure. The condition of affairs in Manila is far from being satisfactory. If we turn to our own country, it will be admitted by all patriots—and the most fervent patriots—that we have swung into a sphere of constant, intermin

able, and dangerous complications. The halcyon days we expected from the election promises of 1895 have not been realised. We have been nearer war with one of the Great Powers of Europe than we have been since Lord BEACONS- FIELD almost urged us into a conflict with Russia. The unsettled questions are many, the negotia- tions are frequent, and important despatches are withheld from the purview of Parliament. We are steadily losing confidence in Lord SALISBURY, though the fillip of Omdurman has assuaged our patriotic griefs for the time being. These are not party statements, but real, hard facts, deplored as much by Conservatives as by Liberals. We are taking over new responsibilities, and our expendi- ture mounts up alarmingly. "Wars and rumours of wars " were to be the precursors of a great uni- versal change. The new century seems likely to come in with anything but peace benefactions and universal concord.

The marvellous outburst of sympathy with Mr. Kipling in his dangerous illness demonstrates afresh the unique power that poets possess of cap- turing the imagination, not of ordinary people alone, but of statesmen, administrators, philoso- phers, and kings. The public sorrow at the death of Lord Tennyson or Robert Browning did not exceed the demonstration of heartfelt sympathy ' with the sufferer at New York. In London and in the States the clergy have spontaneously reques- ted the prayers of the congregations for his re- covery. This is not testimony to the fervour of his work as an Imperialist, but to his power as poet and writer, and to the regret felt that a life of such immense promise should be in danger of extinction. Mr. Kipling has attained a place in the popular affection that can only be compared to that achieved by Dickens, at the same age. His best work can hardly have been accomplished. No other poet or writer at thirty-three shews such un- flagging energy or fertility. He is, moreover, a bond between two _hemispheres, between two people cut off by an ocean, and by an enmity that has lasted nearly a century. Had the matter been referred to popular suffrage, Mr. Kipling would have been Poet Laureate of England ; but he has won a better place than that, and that is the lau- reateship or spokesmanship of all who speak the British tongue. Sometimes his interpretations of the mute aspirat;ons of Anglo-Saxons is faulty, but no other man could interpret them in such rousing language, with the same wonderful ex- pressiveness, no'r, on the whole, so correctly.

The death of Mr. Percival B. Scott is felt with Poignant sorrow by the Liberals of Warrington, to the great majority of whom the news came as a great surprise. Though it was generally known that Mr. Scott was in delicate health, few were aware that that insidious disease,consumption,had been for some time stawly but surely sapping his yitality and bringing him nearer and nearer the Inevitable end. Mr. Scott was a type of man out of the ordinary run of those gentlemen who come to the rescue of a constituency which cannot find ?. local candidate. He was young, comparatively Inexperienced, and unknown to the inhabitants of the town, yet he was undaunted at the odds against him, and cheerfully took up the gage thrown down by Mr. R. Pierpoint. At that time, nearly four years ago, Mr. Scott was far frOm being strong in body, but his pluck was admirable and he fought a good fight gallantly and well. He soen overcame the not unnatural hesitancy of the electors at giving their support to a stranger, and within a few days of his first visit he had won the confidence and esteem of every man he had met. Mr. Scott's ability, enthusiasm, and courage, compelled the admiration of all, while his magnetic charm of manner attracted people to him in every part of the constituency. Success was not vouchsafed him, but though defeated at the poll, he e3tab- lished himself so firmly in the hearts of the Liberal electors that his untimely death at the age of 32 bas left a wound which only time can heal. What- ever the future may have in store for them War- rington Liberals will always honour the memory of the true-hearted gentleman who championed their cause at the general election of '95.

The growth of the foreign and. colonial fruit trade with this country seems at last to have awakened fruit growers at home to a sense of their lost opportuni- ties. We fear there is no excuse to bekput forward in favour of the orchard-owners at home. They have lost trade through carelessness and ignor- ance. They have pulled and packed their fruit in a happy-go-lucky spirit, thinking that as they were So much nearer the consumer would be bound to buy theit products in preference to foreign im- ports. But fruit consumers, like other people, have a strong preference for fruit that is in fine condition. Abroad they have reduced packing to a fine art, with the result that both in looks and flavour foreign apples are put on the market Superior to the products from the orchard districts at home. One would think that an average profit of £l5 an acre would tempt fruit farmers to do the best they could, but when their orchards begin to lose vigour they stand by the very picture of help- lessness, and we get complaints of foreign com- petition, and unfair railway rates. If they planted wisely, cut the orchard grass, tilled the ground scientifically, and studied the art of packing, the industry would flourish. It is estimated that the total outlay on planting need not exceed no per acre, and as a new orchard is supposed under Proper conditions to makr, a handsome profit for forty years, the outlay is not great, nor are the conditions governing the annual profit onerous.

Questions in Parliament with regard to the treatment accorded the Mandi's remains after the battle of Omdurman have not resalted in any riew facts being adduced. Mr. Brodrick made a brief, non-committal reply, and after one or two Pretty strong expressions of opinion from mem- bers the subject dropped. The public is, there- Tere, still without definite information concerning "this horrible and ghastly outrage "as Mr. Bartley termed it, but there is no reason, so far, to dis- credit the reports that one officer secured the Mandi's head, 'mother a finger nail or two, and Others miscellaneous portions of his anatomy. There are military authorities who have approved of this desecration;of the dead, on the ground that it was necesAary to prevent a recrudescence of trouble in the Soudan from those who hold the

ahas remains in superstitious reverence. The excuse, to us, appears trivial, and not in the least - R justification of such barbaric and un-English • Conduct. Surely the power of Britain is equal to the suppression of the Soudanese fanatics without resorting to the mutilation of a dead foe's remains. We hope there will.be some satisfaction obtain- able from the report which Lord Cromer is said to be preparing on the matter.

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYANS AND THE 20TH
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYANS AND THE 20TH
CENTURY FUND.
1318 GUINEAS PROMISED.

The Wesleyans of Runcorn display continued activity in their support of the 20th Century Fund, and on Tuesday evening a highly successful meet- meeting was held at the Wesleyan schoolroom, Weston, the attendance at which was large and en- thusiastic. The chair was occupied by Mr. William Dunbavin,and he was supported on the platform by the Revs.o W L Christien, R J Clifton and J A B Malvern (circuit minieters),Messrs G Bellamy (cir- cuit steward), F J Norman, J P, and Messrs C Tay- lor and J Povah (local secretaries), Excellent speeches upon the fillip and incentive Methodism would receive as a result of the estab- lishing of tne fund, and upon the proposals em- bodied in the scheme for the application of the million guineas, were delivered by the Revs C. W. L. Christien, and R. J. Clifton, Mr. F. J. Nor- man, Mr. George Bellamy, as well as by two local gentlemen (Mesgrs. S. Dodd and J. Lister), and which were most enthusiastically received, it was announced that 131 guineas were promised from Weston alone.

The St. Paul's Church on Thursday night was thronged with a large audience, whose sympathy with the movement was enthusiastically displayed The chief object of the meeting :was the sign- ing of the rolls. We understand that two rolls will be signed, one to go to the headquarters of the Fund, and the other to be preserved with the annals of the circuit, which is very gratifying. The amount of the Fund already promised is given as 1,318 guineas, but possibly by the time these lines appear, it will have passed that figure.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES,
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES,

[BY A CORRESPONDENT] At the Rural District Council meeting.,,,on Tuesday Mr. S. Woodward again referring to the "tuber- culosis agitation" gave utterance to some very im- portant statements, which, more than anything he has hitherto addressed upon the subject, gave a sufficient reason for no immediate action being taken with r-gard to the milk traffic by the Run- corn Rural District Council. The tuberculine test (whatever that 'may mean) came in for a consider- able amount of ridicule; and instances were quoted of valuable cattle having ben condemned by the test; but on a post mortem examination being taken no trace of the disease was found in the animals. If " seientists of the present day" cannot find any pathological reason for this, then the effi- cacy of the test cannot but be held in doubt. Cau- tion is the only measure justifiable whilst a ques- tion of this nature is in its experimental stage.

Mr. John Ashton, the Clerk to the Rural District Council, intimated that the result of his visit to London, last we,ek, where he attended the taxation of the Loudon and North-Western Railway Com- pany Bill in the matter of the Helsby Sewerage, was most satisfactory, The bill which was for £1299 193 I.ld or practically £l3OO, was reduced by £643. This stroke of business on the part of Mr. Ashton was deservedly commended by the Council.

Considerable interest was evinced in the male voice competition at the Widnes Eisteddfod on Thursday week. From the first there was no doubt but that the prize would come to Runcorn—indeed, the general opinion was that "Timmins" were go- ing to win. They were "cock-sure" of the whole thing from the very commencement; and though the decision of the adjudicator did not give uni- versal satisfaction he satisfie 1 the" Timmins' choir so much that they had to vent their jubilation in a congratulatory concert. I should add, however, that the remarks of the aljudicator upon the con- ductor of one of the unsucces4ul choirs,were to say the least anything but complimentary.

Oa Wednesday next, the Public Hall, will be, it is to be hoped, well filled with a happy gathering of the old folks of Runcorn and district, on the occa- sion of their annual treat. It islinderstood that the chairman of the m )vement, Mr. Samuel Taylor, J. 13,., will preside. Nlr.WiLliam Sqaw is resp)nsible for the "buying in " and from what is generally known of his ability in that directioa he can be de- pended upon to provide all that should go to make the treat a real one.

From the remarks made by Mr. Imison, at the Council meeting on Thursday morning, one would surmise that hi 3 attention had been caught by the note referring to" what might be done in the way of assessment." Well, lam not, sorry; and though not disinclined to believe all that Mr. Imison says, still I must call attention to what Mr. J. Wilson says also:—" That he would be glad of some univer- sal basis of assessment, as at present it was a grievous thing and vexed some of them sorely.'" It is evl4ent that there is something unsatisfactory somewhere.

The election of Councillors for the Runcorn Urban District is fixed for the 25th of March, and it will not be long b4ore the old array of qinstions "Baths versus Brea 1," "Electric Light versus Gas Company" etc. etc., will be brought out of their time-honoured retreats; only however, to be laid to rest aftersome- one has secured a lease of three years to a seat in the Town Ball.

Norman, Mrs. Annie Hoose, and her two daughters Mary (12) and Lilly (10), of Church-st., Runcorn, wrs brought up on several charges. Toe first charge gone into was one in which the two girls were cearged with stealing two pairs of boots, value 55., the property of Messrs. Tyler and Song. Cherch-Areet, on the 9th and 10th of February; and the mother was chargeci with receiving the same know- ing them to have been stolen.—From theevielence it ap- peared that Charles Harris, manager for Messrs: Tyler, missed the boots (produced) which he identified by the nrivate mark and other signs, on the 9:h of February. On the following he missed another pair, in consequence of whieh he gave inform ition to the police.—Police- Constable Samuel Gregory demsed to searching the defendant's house in Church-street, in comnany with Sergeant Brewster and Constable H. Fry. Mrs. [loose kept a sweet shop in Churce-street, almost directly opposite to Tyler's. The boots were found is the house; the pair that Harris identified being found in a clipboard. Subsequently he charged the prisoners. The girl :Mary replied "I took them"; Lilly said "I was with her At the time." In answer to the charge of receiving the boots Mrs. Floosie sail "All I am aware of beine et :len are the boots from Tyler's shop,Mr. Gregory."—Mrs. Homo, said what the Conetab'e stated was quite correct.—Electing to be Summarily dealt with the three prisoners pleaded guilty to oise pair.—Bef ore sentence was given it was de- cided to go into the other charges, and take them collec- tively. Prisoners were then charged, the girls with stealing, and the mother with receiv ngenveo pairs cof slippers.anci two pairs of boots between the 20th and 25th of February, the prererty of the Runcorn Industr'al Co- operative Society Limited—they all pleaded ignorance of the aff sir.—Mr. J. Ellio t,me.nager of the boot and shoe department of the Co-operative Society Stores, testified to missing the articles, but stated he could only now identify the slippers. He could not identify the boots. —P.C. Gregory stated that he foand the articles on the same oecasien as that in the previous case. One of the girls was wearing a pair of the stolen slippers. In answer to the charge of receiving them and stealing them the prisoners made no reply. Prisoners were further charged with stealing a doll, 8 pecket knives, a mite, toy toilet set, artificial plant, toy perambulator, and a violin (valued at aboet 15s. 61.), the properties of Mr. G Moores, Regent-street, on several occasions.—Mrs. Moores, wife of Mr. G. Moores, toy dealer and watchmaker, Regent-street, identified the goods as belonging to her husband.—Constable Fry (thr nieh whose instrumentality the prisoners were found out) s'ated from information received from the last wit- ness he instituted inquiries. He saw the prisoner Lilly Hoose ancrac to gn to Mr. Moore'e shop, and asked hcr her name. She replied " Poly Jones from Waterloo-street, Runcorn." As he happened to know Polly Jones he told the girl she had , given the wrong name, whereupon she commenced Ito cry. He then questioned her as to whether she hail been to the shop before ? Whether she had t +ken anything, out of it? and whether she was accom- panied be anyone e'se ? To which questions she I answered" yes" and said she was accompanied by her I sister Mary and had taken a trinket set and some pccket I knives. He asked when) the aricles were ? and she I said nlf you come with me I will show you ?" Subse- quently he went with her and found most of the articles Produced, as well as a portion of another trinket son in premises at the back of the house. Her sister also came out and put sometking. into his hand; on looking at it he found she had given him a shilling: He asked where she got it and she replied "Mamma gave it me for you." He afterwar is asked Mrs. Hones about the shilling and she said she give it the little girl to give to him. He returned her the money; and after the place had been searched in the manner already drncribed the prisoners were takes to the Police Station. In answer to the charge Mary said " I have stolen some, and Lily has takevi the others." The mother said she knew nothing about them.

Aw.werurg to the offences collectively. Mrs Hoose and Mary noose pleaded not guilty, and Lilly Howe guilty. Annie noose, (the mother) stated she did not know anything of the articles stolen, only the one pair of boots from Tyler's, and when the little girl Lilly brought them in he wanted her to gn back with them. But the littb girl carried on sl, and burst out screaming and cry- ing that she thought it would be best to say nothing about them and let it Wow over. She was sorry now. however, that she had not done so. because she Was su eit would have caused less troub,e.—Mary Hoose said she had only taken the one pair of boots which ehe saw he.neing out of the ,door.—The Magistrates Clerk: (addressing the children) : Girls. Din't you know you are riling wrong in taking these things? Both girls : Yes sir. The Chairman said it was ridiculous for the prisoner Annie Room to say she knew nothing about it. She m”st have known the children were stealing. Prisongr interposing said she knew they had Wren one pair, bat never saw the others until she saw them on the table in the court. div.head: RUNCORN CHARACTER SKETCHES. No. 2.
div.p: RUNCORN CHARACTER SKETCHES. No. 2.

When Napoleon uttered that memorable sentence which was to the effect that the English were " a nation of shopkeepers" he hit the truth of the matter in a most appropriate phrase and expressed a truth which was even deeper than he was aware Britain in its earliest days was noted for its traders and its commerce. The glimpses which are obtainable of the customs of our forefathers pro- claim them to have been essentially primitive shop- keepers. Whether this spirit of trading origina- ted in our primitive home—Sleswick—is impos- sible to say. But it is a -noticeable fact, that a spirit of enterprise has always been one of the chief characteristics of the race. We are not therefore surprised to find that the spirit increased with the growth of the population, and that its animating inSuence is found to-day, largely distributed over the English speaking race. It would, consequently, be strange indeed if in the smallest village town there was not to be found a type of the men whe have contributed so largely to the greatness of the "inviolate Isle." If it be admitted that enterprise has made ngland what she is to-day, and if it be also admitted that competition the natural sequence of enterprise,pro- motes commercial prosperity,tne man under notice has benefited Runcorniane in tne best possible way, and therefore deserves the gratitude of all, tie is in many respects a self-made man. His business when he assumed the direct management had not the gigantic proportions which it has at the present time. From very small begin- ning it has grown step by step owing to the assiduous attention bestowed upon it. It would not be too much to say that he is the smartest business man Runcorn has produced. The man who can `• best "him must, we should think, be a com- pound of the canny Scotchman and the wily Jew and fully deserves the compliment of being called " shrewd." Ever on the water), he take the utmost advantage of the passing moment, and throws into his work an enthusiasm and energy which are the sure forerunners of success. It is, doubtless, owing to his love of competition that the poorer classes of our town are enabled to buy so cheaply •' the bread which perisheth." Never before in the history of Runcorn have the necessaries of life been so cheaply sold. Thus the indigent and needy, partly owing to the exertion of this wholesale caterer for the bodies, have the physical wants supplied for sums as far removed from famine prices as the east is from the weer,. It would not be safe h3wever to assert that the community has been thus benefitted from a purely disinterested motive. We believe that a certain amount of the selfish element has entered into the plans of this individual. But we also believe that the man has yet to be found who lives solely for the benefit of his fellows. The love of self is engrained in the hearts of all men. In the public duties of the town he has rendered yeoman service. Ie the committee, on the plat- form, in the council chamber, in the private room, he strenuously advocates the principle of progress. Undoubtedly he is an extremist in his views, but what man has ever accompliehed great things unlees he were a fanatic in the cause he championed? It will by this statement be surmised, and correctly too, that he is much averse in being kept in the back-ground. lie must be a leader or he must be nothing. Other men may be cootent to elide down the stream of life pulled by tee leading strings of others,but the "man of indepen.lent mind' will spin a line for himself. If he is not born to command he is certainly born to stimulate the nerves of his less courageous companions. it may be his physical appearance adds to his mental power of influencimg those with whom he comes in contact. Tall, broad shouldered, every limb well proportioned, a good carriage and com- manding presence, it will be seen that nature has bestowed her gilts somewhat lavishly, with the result that he appears to advantage among his townsmen. It is, of ceurse, but natural that a man so physically endowed should be passionately devoted to athletics. Not only is he a sturdy sup- porter of various kinds of recreation—especially of our national winter pastime—but, we believe that he is no mean athlete hiinself. In the seasons he takes en active interest in all athletic sperts, and it is worthy of note that he is one of the finest eques- trians for ne'les round. The Football Club has especial need t) be indebted to him. The ragged urchins too who surround the gates at the foot- ball field may well shout in the exuberance of their joy " He Comes ! lie comes !" Not only is he a man of the world but he is in every respect a society man. Social gatherings re- ceive a very large share of his attention. It is almost unnecessary to odd that he is "Hail fellow, well met at every one." We will not assert that he carries this too far, hut we do assert everyone should be" temperate in all things." If there is one characteristic which distinguishes him from other men, it is his intense fondness for practical jokes. Perhaps there are few people who have not at some time or other been the victim of a practical joke. it is perhaps difficult to conceive anything more objectionable than this form of sport, carried on as it is at the expense of your neighbout's feelings. While everyone can admire sport in which two or more can join, the persons are few indeed who can smile when the joke is against themselves.And,most won- drousthinge the practical joker is mroriOus in this respect. No sooner is a Roland given for his Oliver, than he becomes highly indignant and cannot see for the life of him the force of the j nee. The in- dividual under notice is a type of this man. Seeing the disastrous consequences which sometimes fol- low from this prone lure, we would counsel all per- sons in good faith to abstain frpn practices which bring little "grist to the mill" and heap nought but discredit upon themselves. Le, tinr,e the cat among the pigeons may be all right for the cat but must be extremely disagreeable to the less offensive animals. To his honour, however, it must be said that he is extremely generous and warm-hearted. And many an old resident, and many a bare- footed waif have been the recipients of his bounty. As is usual with those who are generous to a fault, he is extremely erratic and impulsive. Conequentry his actions are made the shuttle-cock of conflicting opinions Were he described,however, as " unstable as water" the remark would be but is betrayal of ignorance. for in many matters he is caeable of evincing a determination second to none. It is patent to all that his weak point lies in allowing himself to be too easily influenced by °there. It is to this failing that several errors of judgment must be ascribed. It cannot be said literature is one of his strong points. Book knowledge occupies a very insignifi- cant position in the list of his accomplishments: But his intimate acquaintance with the book of human nature makes up, in some degree, for this defect.

Though no orator—nor cm he be even said to possess any elocutionary power—he never- theless appeals with more than ordinary success to the public by directing his attention to the funny sile of humanity. He is more of a wit tha,n a humorist, and some of his flashes are indeed very fin. His temper is by no means a desirable one. It is far too much like gunpowder to be safe for any length of time. Quick to take offence, he is led into actions over which he repents at leisure.
After a close analytical examination, the conclu- sion must be drawn that he is as fins a specimen of British pluck and manliness as could be found in a journey from Lands End to Jnhn 0' Groats.

EPIGRAM. A man of wolh who woold aspire. Te raise his townsmen's joys the higher. Though sprinkled with frivolity, Too fond perhaps of jolity With all his faults none ere should tire, To seek his best and that admire.

div.head: HEALTH OF RUNCORN. MEDICIL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF RUNCORN. MEDICIL OFFICER'S ANNUAL REPORT.

Dr. F. McDougall, Medical Officer of licalth for Run- corn, has just issued his report for the year ending Dec. 31st, 1898. He states that three hundred and eleven notificitions were received during the yeor, as comparel with 233 re- ceived during the previous year, an iicrease of 28. Tois increase is accounted for by a considerable increase of tbe Diptlenitic notifications as compared with last year. SCARLET FEVER: Is represented by 14 cases, as com- pared with 93 eases for 1897,and 97 cases for 1896, a net decrease on the previous year of 75 cases. Twenty-four cases of enteric fever were notified during the year, as compared with twenty-four cases notified during 1887, and 22 during 1896. Nineteen houses were affected. Thirtrfive nottfieations of continurd fever were re- ceived, affecting 30 h mr,es. Twenty nAlfinations of continued fever were receive.l during 1897. There are no deaths under this heal. Fifteen cases of erisipelas were notified during the year, las against twenty-two cases notified during 1897, ' and twenty-five cases notified duriug 1896. A net &- crease of seven cases over 1897. For ttie last four years there has been going on a steady and gratifying diminu- tion in the number of cases of erysipelas notified. Two cases of croup were no:A.I during the year, two cases wera notified during 1897, and fo.ir cases for 1896. Three cases ef puerperal lever were notified, and two cases were notified fur the previous rar. 'f,vo hundred and twenty-two notifications were received of diph- theria, as against one hundred and twenty-one notifica- tions received during the preceding y 'ar. January fur- nishel fourteen cases involving tuirte.-n houses, two of thesis cases were imported ; Fe3ruAry, wirty-one notifi- cations, notifying thirty c ,ses and involving twenty-six houses ; in March twenty cases were nctified involving sixteen houses ; in April seventeen cases involving thir- teen houses (one case reported as diphtheria proved on further investigation to be due to another caus?). May, six notifications received one in duplicate,involving five houses. June, twenty nqific stions were received invol- ving fifteen houses, .makieg •total for the first six months of he year of one hundred and eight cases. For the second half of the year one hundred and fourteen notifications were reeeived,tvrenty-three for July involv- ing sixteen houses ; five br August involving four houses; twenty-two for September involving sixteen houses ; thirty-two for October involving twenty-seven houses ; twenty-two for November involving eighteen houses ; and ten for December involviag six houses,
MORTALITY RETURNS.

The number of deaths from all causes registered within the Authorities Sanitary District during the year 1898 arno Juted to three hundrid and thirty-one, as compared with three hundred and thirty-eight for the year 1897 a decrease of seven on the previous year, two hundred and sixty-eicitat for the year 1896,and three hundred and ninety for 1895. I regret to onserve that the infant death-rod of one year ar,cl under continues to head the list, and amounts to ninety, a decrease of eighteen on the previous year, which is represented by one hundred and eight. 'Sixty two of these d lathe were re4istered during the last six months of the year, September heal- ing the list with seventeen. Fifty-nine daates of one year and under five years were registered during the year, as compared with seventyeene deaths registered during the preceding year, a decrea,e of twelve. Thirty- four deaths of five years and uader fifteen years were regi-t !red. Fifteen deaths under the same heading were tegistere i during 1897, making an increase of nineteen. Ten deaths of young p-rsoos of fifteen years and under twenty-five years were registered as compared with fifteen under the same head registered during the pre- ceding year, a decrease of five. Eighty-seven deaths of twenty-five and under sixty-fl ve years were registered dur- ing the year, and for 1897 nil:l,4y deaths were registered under the same heading, a decrease of three. Ffty-one deaths of persons of sixty-five years and upwards were registered, and forty-one deaths of persons in the same class were registered during the previous year, an in- crease of tan making a grand total for toe year of three hundred and thirty-one. The death rate for the year I am glad to say is calculated on a slight increase in the population; for several years past the death rate had to be calculated on a falling off in the population. lam however assurod by those best acq sainted with the Letting of property in the town, that bowies are letting better, and that unoccupied houses are to some extent getting slowly occupied; taking the fac's into considera- tion, and also the excess of births over deaths, I think I may fairly assume that the population as at midsummer of lest year would be eighteen too is ancl;taking eighteen thousand as the p3pulation the death rate for the year would be 183 per thousand, and if the twenty-seven deaths classed under the head of " injuries" and referred to in ay.ocher paragraph be deducted, it will leave three hundred and four deaths to be accounted far, and give a death rate of 16 8 per thousand as the general death rate for the year.

Twenty-seven deaths are classed under the head of injuries, as against fiLeen for the previous years, this class always iorm ; a subject of a coroners ioquriv and is invariably due t 3 sudden or violent death. Dierrhoel and dysentery are credited with twilit e-three deaths, twenty-two of these death 3 were of children and infants of five years or under (as c )mpered with tweetc-eme deaths for 1897), three of these deaths were registered in July, five in August,and ten in September. Seven cl,a•les were registered from phthisie, as compared with sixceee deaths registered from the same CAllse during the pr-vi- Gus year, or a decrease of nine on the year. All wete persons of five years or upwards. Forty-four deaths were registered from bronchites.pleurisy,end pheumoni' e as compared w.t'a fitte-ewe deans registe- med from the ' same cause during 1897. Twenty-two of these deaths were of children under five years and twenty-two were of persons of five years and upwar is. Whooping cough is not represented in the death re urns. Fourteen notifi- cations of scarlet fever were received and only onedeath, the death taking place the last week in December. It is very satisfactory to fled that what was formerly regarded as a local habitant and a scourge, is now gradually disappearing, and at the moment of wr tints there is not a sing e case in the town' and there has not been for some time. I belisve that this state of things is in a great part due to a full appreciation by parents of the need of isolation during the descpetneting per o of the disease, and to other useful measures of precau- tion, not oßly is this advantageous in the interests of the commenity, but is very much so in the int-rests of the unfortunate sufferer. There is els an increasine dispesi- tinn on the pars of parents to carry out more fiscally tee injunctions ot the Medical Adviser, as well as that of the Authority, which is highly gratifying to all cencernecl. There were fifteen notifications of eresipelee and no deaths. Measles is not a notifiahle di ease. There are three deaths registered from this cause, one in June, one in July, and one in Augurt, ell tender flee years of age. Five deaths were registered fr un membranous croup,' two cases were notified, and for °nee the deeths under this head exceed by three the number notifi-d. Four deaths from enteric fester were registered during the ee,-ar, one in August, two in September, and one in October, all of five years or uowerds, a high death rate for the number of netificat,one received. Oee death was returned as due to influenz I, which oceurrill in April last, and there are nine deaths recorded ac due to heart disease, twenty-two deaths were returned under toe same head for 1897. P,urperal fever is not represented in the death rate although three eases were notified, one of the three cases notified died, but the death was not attribeted to the case notifiel, and is returned under the heading of "all other dice tses." One hundred and seventy deaths were returned under this heading, sevehty-two under five years, and ninety-eight five years and upwards. The only satisfactory feature in this re- turn is the reduction ie the death rate of children under five years of are over the p-eeeding year. E•enty-four deaths were returned in 1897 of children under five years of age, and sixty-four represented by five years and up- wards. The number of notifications of diphtheria re- ceived are referred to in a former paragraph of this re- port, thirty-seven deaths from this terribly fatal disease are registered, and the deaths are pretty evenly distri- buted over the who!e year. A very low percentage of deaths for the cases notified.

The thirty seven deaths registered as due to this fat d form of disease, represents a very low rate of mortality indeed, and is very strong evidence of the exceedingly mild character of the majority of cases notified, if they be true diptheria, but this difficeicy could only be settled by a bacteriolosic al examination of the throat secretions, and the expense of this method of investigation is prohi- bitive, and the result of such examination in some instances might not be Conclusive nor too satisfactary. The beginning of the epidemic dste4 beck as far as mid- summer of 1897. The question of the or at of the epidemic is d scufsed very tally in the report for that year, and what was supposd to be the chef cau re of the origin of the epidemic cannot now be held to be opera• tive for 1898 The drainage q iestion has bens pretty freely discussed, insanitary conditions have been in- quired into, and although in a few instances certain defects were discovered and remedied, this hardly acceunts for the continuance of the epidemic, with cer- tain lapses, during the whole year. Prior to the con- struction of ths Menchester Ship Canal, much the larger portion of the township was drained by one or other of six separate sewers that had their outlets, with the exception of two on the shore of the river Mersey. These sewers during tow tides, at their outfalls at all events, get well ventilated, and no doubt a certain amount of clean pure air entered in this way. These six separate sewers since the construction of the Ship Canal have their outfalls into an intercepting sower (de,cribed by Mr. Wilding, engineer and surveyor to the aa' herity), in a letter addressed to myself,and cenvertine what were once six separate sewers, into one sewer. Unfortunately the intercepting sewer for a good part of its length gets waterlogged during tidetime twice in the twenty-four hours, and more so with a heavy rainfall and high tides, and consequently the air pressure in these sewers is in- creased. An effort is being made to lessen the gss pres- sure in the sewers, by placing ventilating s'aafts over the upper reaches of the sewers, these shafts have been placed where high pressure is Inevitable. No doubt a further distribution will be made ewe the shafts placed in suitable lonilities. I in Tee•ei cluing the fall of the year together with Mr. Wilding and Mc. Percival, nuisance inspector, the intercepting sewer at the

outlets, and with the exception of an out- let that enters into the old portion of the intercepring sewe^, the Fewer generally was found remarkably clean and free from silt. I had occasion to investigate the presence of Dipthera in five different houses in the east end of the t own, connected by family ties, and whose members were admittedly co-mingling together daily. There is no doubt in my own mind that the evil had spread from house to house. Remonstrances count for little in these cases and a toffee stick or tin whistle becomes th 3 property of common ownership. I observed durine, the whole of the year a remerkable freedom from this scourge amongst the families of cer- tain members of our community, who send their chil- dren to one school and there were only three children of school age notified as scholars of this school during the whole year. To my mind this points very strongly to the probability that co-minglings at school have been chiefly responsib!e for the continuance of the epidemic. I am making a communication to the Health CAnmittee to ask them to take steps to serve notice on toe pareets of all children of school age in respect of whem notifica- tions have been received cautioning them against send- ing the children back to school until after the expiration of a m ,nth at least, after absolute recovery. And also to communicate with the School Board asking that authority to caution the school visitors against pressing parents to send their children back to school. Also that notice be served upon all head teachers recommending them to be furnished with a health certificate from a duly qualified medical man before the re-admission of a child after convalesence from diptheria. Also that a weekly list of infected children be furnished to the School Board Clerk for the use of the School Board Visi- ters this I think is a preferable method of dealing with children of school age rather than suggest that the Scheols should Me visited to examine the children for suspected cases. This species of " School Hunt " would not commend itself to parents, and an examination without their conseat might make an Examiner liable for an assault. I trust these suggestions will meet the difficulty, and that pannts will try to work with the authorities in ridding the town of a very unwelcome visitor.

The infant rate of mortality continues high, but there is a considerable decrease °a last year, ninety deaths of one year or under were regis ersd, one hundred and eight were registered in the same eass during 1897, or a decrease of eighteen on the year. There is still con- siderablß room for improvement.

BIRTH RATE. Five hundred and seventy births were registered dur- ing 1898, five hundred and eights-three were registered during 1897, or a decrease on the year of thirteen ; two hundred an.l forty-nine births in excess of deaths, the birth rate for 1898 would be 316 ar.cording to the estim- ated population. The birth rate for 1897 was 33.3
MILK SUPPLY.

Attention at considerable leagtti was called in my last report to the storage of milk, and to the more modern methods of dealing with it before it is supplied a 3 food to infants, and it is only necessary her() to remind parents how much they can do in this way for their little ones. On the 4'h of November, 1697, the Authority memorialised the County Council to establish a Bacteri• ological Laboratory for the County; since then the ques- tion of tuberculosis in catle, ani kindrod diseases in man, has been taken up in very influential quarters,and no doubt something will be done in time in the matter by legiilation. Neighbouring authorities are seeking powers by legislation to deal with this great evil in their own way, and if these powers ar . obtained, will no doubt prove a drastic remedy for a real and crying evil. The memorial is annexed for a reprint. REPORT OF INSPECTOR OF NUISANCES.

Mr. James Percival, Inspector of Nuisances, pr—esents in a concise form his annual report, which gives the fol- lowing among other particulars :--Nui-ances discovered 292 ; nuisances abated, 280. The following is a descrip- tion of some of the nuisances dealt with :—Defective drains, 17 ; ctWred drains, 11 ; dcfactivetrapped gullies, 19 ; defective waste water-pipes from sink stones, 11 ; ash-pits removed and ash-boxes provided, 43; structural alterations to ash-pits and privies, 3 ; defective and un- paved yards and passages, 9 ; houses ov,rcrowded, 5 ; houses filthy, 4 ; houses vvito filthy close,,s, 3 ; howe without proper ventilation. 1 ; houscs without proper water supply, 5 ; houses with stagnant water lying in ccllar, 4 ; accumulation of manure, 13 ; decayed fruit and fish, 7 ; smoke nuslnces, 9 ; rniscellanroas, 36. The supervision of milkshops and cowsheds has been regular, and only in one instance has there been cause for complaint._

The superviA4n of registered common lodging houses has been regular, and no cause for complaint. During. the year one person was prosecuted for keeping unregis- terei lodging house and fined 53 and 143 61 costs. During the year two persons have been prosecuted for allowing the chimneys of their dwelling-houses to be on ore, and fined is and 84 61 ^ostg. o....•••■llllmiosis

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.

A TYPICAL STREET ARAB. On Monday at the Warrington Borough Police Court, before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates Alfred Beckat (16), known as' Lawyer "Beckett, residing at a lodging house in Friars'-green,was charged with com- mitting a breach of the peace in the Market Place on February 22nd.—P.C. Clough said hu saw defendant assaulting another boy, who was much taller, but youngfr. The officer stopped him, and defendent "com- menced using impudence." He called the officer" a big fool," and " a big head." (Langhter.)—The Chair- man were you afraid of him? (Laughter.) You did not need aagistance. (Laughter).--3 he Chief Constable said defendint was "a little rip." He was a nuisance in the market. He was a street Arab, and Mr. Taylor could say something about him.—P.S. Cheney stated that defendant did not Alva with his parents.—The Chairman : What have you tl s-iy for threatening thi3 policeman ?—Defendant said he had nothing to say.— The Chief Constable stated that defendant: had been be- fore the court for a breach of the peace, fighting and for gambling, and bad had three days in the cells.—Tne Clerk (Mr. White) :—Are you willing to go to Dr Bar- nardo's home ?-IMendast : Na, I'll go to my father! —The Chief Constable: It's the lodging-house or the gutter for him.—Mr. Taylor said that when defendant had to go to school he was c3atinually before the C3urt for non-atteniance. He was a pest in the streets, and obtained his living in the market or at the atatioos.—The Chairman said defendant would be kept in custody unti 6 p.m.

"RUSHING" A PUBLICAN. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday before Alderman Sutton (in the chair), and other magis- trates John Cody, 27, Bank-strcet, who appeared in the dock with his head covered with bandages, was charged with having been drunlt and disorderly ie Bank-stret, 10.45 p.m. on Saturday.—P.C. Cooper said he saw a large crowd of people oeposite tins" Bird-in-Hand," Bank-street. He proceeded there, and found defendant lying drunk in the lobby of the public-house. The land- lord (Mr. Reddington) asked witness to put defendant out, and when he did so defendant became disorderly. There was a large wound on his head,and witness band- aged it when he got to the Police Szatioe. Subsequently he took him to the Infirmary, where he had, until that morning, been attended as an in-patient. The door of the public-heuse was broken.—Mr. Reddington stated that en Saturday night he refused to serve two men as they were drunk. Defendant afterwards came to the house in a similar condition, and witness also refused to serve him. Defendant then called up the other two men, and they "rushed "him. The door was smashed open, and the piece of wood produced was part of the door. He found defendant lying on the floor bleeding and he sent for a policeman. In answer to the Chief Constable, witness said he did not strike the dEfendant with a poker.—The Chief Constable (producing a small piece oi wood), said there was blond on it, but the defendant ,might have bumped his head against it. However, what- ever he bad done he had been well punisni d for it, and, perhaps, the Bench would take that fact into considera tion.—The Chairman: Yes, he seems to have been punished enougla.—Further questioned, he said he knew nothing about being locked up.—The Chairman : Well, let this be a warning to 7ou. The case will be dismiseed. THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF DRIVERS. At the Borough Police Court,on Monday, before Alder- man Sutton (in the chair) and othi r magistrates, Jeep jabesee, 37. Stafford-road, was summoned for having on the I.stri February illtreated a horse by werking it whilst it was in an unfit condition. He pleaded guilty. —P.C. Johnson said he was on duty in Bridge-street at 2.45 p.m. on the day in question when he saw the de- fendant in charge of a grey mare attached to a van. The animal had two large wounds on its shoulders, and he told the di fondant to take it out of the shafts. The wounds were festering. One wound was five inches long and three inches wide.—lnspector Canning (R.S.P.O A.) also gave evidence, atd said the animal was not in a fit condition to work.—The Chairman said the defendant was to blame, and he would be fined 10a. and costa.—Jemes Ross, 20,Queen-street, was summoned for a similar offence committed on the 15:h February.. He also pleadei guilty.—P.C. Taylor said the derendant was in charee of two horses which belonged to the Car- riage Company. One of the animals was unfit to work, and it was sent back to the stables, and the manager of the company sent another horse out in its place. Defend- ant: The horse appeared to be all right when it came out. When I found that the collar touched the wound I got a pad to cover it.—The manager of the company said that every seryant had strict instructions not to use a horse unless.it was in ggod cendition. The horse was taken out of a dark stable, and is condition might not have been no iced.—TheChairman . We have only i to deal with the driver, who s legally responsible, and who will now be fined ss. and costs.

THE CHAIRMAN AND VACCINATION.—Frank Owen, of Whitley Superior. was granted an order for his child to be exempted from vaccination —Sandy Woodward, of Whitley Superior, applied for a similar order on behalf of his child He said he thought vaccination did chillren more harm than good. His eldest son had never been well since he had been vaccinated. The Chairman: Would you rather run the risk of your child's life by not having it vaccinated? Applicant: Yes I The Chairman: And the rest of your family, too? Applicant: Yes I I never was vaccinated, and I believe if vaccination was done away with there would be more healthy people in the land. The Chairman : What you have said is a fearful thing. I should like to influence your mind in this matter. A'ter the Chairman had given a few illustrations of cases, he asked applicant to go home and think the matter over more seriously. Applicant; If Igo home I shall not have the child vaccinated. The Chairman said it was with great sorrow he signed the order. A CORRE-SPONDENT of the" Ashton Reporter" recently proceeded to 88, Manchester-road, Hyde, and enquired for Mr. Edward Wood, who, it was rumoured, had had a severe attack of paralysis. This is the story related by Mr. Wood. "I am seventy-aix sears of age. For some years I suffered from sciatica, and doctors at- tended me, hut I became worse. A young man advised me to try Dr. Williams* Pink Pills for Pale People,and I did so; soon I began to feel bet- ter, and after taking five boxes I threw my sticks away. I was able to get hack to my work after having been helpless for months. "Then my health kept good until I had a stroke of paralysis,which seless. I lay like a log in bed for _

over a month. I feft myself gradually sinking, when my wife said : • We'll try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills again.' She got a box, and in less than a fortnight I felt much stronger, while after a month had elapsed I could use my limbs and get about the house. That was the result of seven boxes. Since then I ' have been able to walk up tote barber's and I help in the shop again now. I regard my eura as miraculous, for I never ex- pected to come downstairs again. Wny, it was reported three times that I was dead."

Mr. Judd ( says the " SalforAl Chronicle '') residing at 64, Robert Ball-street, Salford. is a strong, well set-up young fellow. EKce.llent wea'h-r favoured ths game between these teams played at Wil lersp3ol, on Stturday, in the" A" team; comp4ition. Tee home team were without the services of Townend, who went with the first team to Brouthton. The c)mpasition of the teams was as f -Mows :—Wsrrington : Bostow, full back ; Moores, Ratc'iffe, Hriclenhull, and Duckworth, three-quarters ; Allen an Bate, halves: Jollev, Skelhorn, Elm, Deakin. Wilcoclzs, Hatton, Hill. Cunningham, forwards: Brough- ten : Hogg. full Inch ; J Lewis, F L3WiC, Wheeler, Conp3r, three-qutrters ; Nelson and Daniels, halves ; Brown, Duffy, rlardisty. Tiffin, Handley, Locke. Aspden and Havea.f3rward4,—Th4 treme team kicked off before abut 2,000 spectators. Neither side had much ad van-

tage in regard to climatic Conditiens, for, though War- rington had the wind against them the visitors had the sun in their eyes. Play rued even during the opening stages of the game. The Warrington men were smart on the ball but seemed unable t 3 gather it. The visitors paid a brief incursion be the Warrington end, but it was only brief, and the homestere forced play back into their opponents' territery, and inunedlatly in front of goal. Here, the exhibition by the home forwards was deplor- able, and chance after chance was missed of getting over until play finally settled back to centre. Allen with a free kick, transferred play to the visitors' territory and Elockenhull punted into the corner. Duckworth fol- lowed up smartly and upset the Brnuetton back, and another good chance was missed by Bate who mulled a pass. Play again travelled back to centre, and a little before half-time Ratcliffe had a free k'ck from a fair position but failed t 3 score. So far, the play bad peen —to say the least oi it—uninteresting. The visitors had demonstrated their supertority in the forward line, but the Warrington men though unable to take passes were playing with more cohesion than their opponents. With the change of ends a elight el-lenge was made in the disposition of the home team. Hocken• hull went on the wing aEd Duckworth was moved to centre. Warrington presscd at the re-commencement of hostilities and the ball was taken in front of the Broughton goa!, and Bate bungled a pass. Hogg relieved the pressure and the effort seemed useless bet it had its lesson. Shortly after the home team again laid siege to their opponents' line, and Allen getting possession threw over Bate's head to Duckworth, who transferred to Hockenhull, and the latter . got over. Ratcliffe kicked for gcal and only missed by a few inches. Warrington I kept up the pressure but were unable to increase their score for some time. Allen however, secured and break- ing through the press, passed to Eden who grounded. Ratcliffe from a favourable position added another two points. The game appeared to be telling on the War- rington forwards at this juncture, and the visiting forwards getting away wi'h the ball BO3COW was hard pressed but he got in his kick. Wheeler secured and put in a fine run but Hockenhull checked hi a career knocking him into touch. Warrington recovered the lost ground and the visitors again forced play in front of the home goal but a forward pass spoiled their chance of scoring. Continuing the pressure Broughton took the ball well up to the goal posts where one cf them crossed the line. The goal kick was successful. The hemesters had somewhat the beat of the play up to time but noth- ing further was scored. Result: Wareneton, 1 goal, 2 tree (8 points) ; Broughton, 1 goal, 1 try (5 points). WARRINGTON ST. ELPIIIN'S V. KIIIKDALE.—This fix- ture was contested at Howley oa Saturday, The visitors won the toss and R. P,orpoint started against the sun. Play was taken to the visitors' end, but Morgan sent the locals back, and play went into the Saints' half. Robson was called upon in rapid succession, until a goal kick relieved the pressure, and Frank Singleton tricked his man and dr;lobled to the other end, but when the oppor- tunity came to shoot he failed distinctly. Play was taken to midfield, the Liverpool team showing some pretty passing both with foot and head. The Saints were slowly being forced to their own goal, and after about 15 minutes' play Kirkdalo onened the scaling, the shot completely baffling Robson. This succeis enlivened both sides, and pretty work was exhibited b each set ut forwards. Give and-take play followed, and ultim- ately St. Elphin's inada a raid on the visitor?! goal, but their efforts were in vain, only corners resulting. The S dots again attacked, and when R mer Pierp)int had the goal at his mercy he handled it. Not t 3 be daunted the Saints made another attempt to equalize, and this time they were successful, for Taylor sent in a last shot, which til3 visiting custodian had no c'iance to save. Half-time, one goal each. Resuming, Kirk late took the ball to the S. Eiphin's goal, and Glover was responsible for eff.cting a grand cle.dta.nc?. Not satisfied with this, the visit-Ts again attacked, and Robson leavin; his goal allowed his visitors to o.otain the lead. S. E!phin's now pressed, and shots were raine i upon the Birkdaie goal. but no points were obtained. A corner was given to St. Elphin's and Jones placed it well, but Morgan cleared, and for the rest of the game Kirkda'e pressed, during %hich time, they scored again. Final :—Kirkdale, three goals ; St: Eiphin's one goal. WIGAN CUP TIE. EARLESTOWN V. BAMFIIRLONG:

For the third time within the space of six we)lrs, the above teams attempted to p'ay off the 2nd round ot the above Cup. On the first occasion when the mateh was played at Bamfarlong, Earlestown won by a solitary goal, but at the meeting of the Afsceeration Committee which was held the week after, the • referee, to the sur- prise of all concerned, state I that he had only allowed the match to be played as a friendly, and oa the second oleasion (also played at liamfurlone). Bamiurlong won by 5 goals to four, but Earlestown protested against the length of the ground, and the match was eventually ordered to be replayed at Earlestown. As considerable feeling had been exhibited by theplayers in the two pre- vious encounters, neutral linesman were appointed, and about five minutes after the appointed time for the start, referee Laithwaite whistled the men into position as follows Earleerown : Goal, Chew ; back, Hayes and Wilkin- son ;half-backs, Green, Parr. and Alldridge : forwards, Smith. Lee, Heusi:mu. Leach and SAVE). Bamfarlong : Goal, Taylor ; backs. Withington and Green ; half-backs, Woods, Houghtoe and Rudd ; tor- warder, Robinson, Magnet!, Linton, Byrne and M 'The weattaer was he ,utifully fine and Hampson started on behalf of the homest3rs in the presence of about 1,700 spectators, and down hill. The bomesteri eery became dangerous but Withington relieved. By the aid of a series of fouls the visitors troubled the Earlestown de- fence. but Parr came to the rescue with a huge kick and Earlestown were soon again swarming railed Taylor. Ira the end however, the visiting defence prevailed and play becamo yeey open, neither side claiming any ma- terial advantage. At leagth Smith sprinted off down the wing but he called forth groans from the speetators by sending the leather yards wide. From the ensuing goal kick Linton gained possersion and pessld to Robin- son, who in turn passed to Magnell, and the latter shot into Chew's hands. The goalkeeper threw the ball away, and Linton met it and shot hard against the crossbar. After this narrow escape, the homesters seemed to reuse themselves and they gave the Bamfurlone defence an anxfous time, shot after shot being very luckily charged down by the backs. The visitors next had a look in,but try as thy woeld, they failed to nierce the home de- fence. From now to the interval play was mostly con tested in the home half. Half time :No score.

On resuming the homesters warmed to their -work ad they were not long in opening the account. 531119 pretty combination enabled Earlestown to find a footing in the visitors' territory and the ball eventually coming to the root of Leach, this nlayer made no mistake and gave Taylor no chance with a lov3ly shot. Encouraged by this success the homesters again took up the attack and once or twice the Barnfurlong goal had very narrow es- capes. Play now became very rough and the referee had to ctuti4a one or two of the players for unnecessary roughness. Leach and Settle were next prominent with a neat passing movement up the wins ; the former player touched Ilia ball to Rampson and he in turn passed to Parr who banged the ball into the net, thus scoring the home team's second goal. Roused hy these reveries the tisitora went down with a rush,and the ball was eventually put into the net through a host of players. This goal sh;uid never have been scored is according to the resumption time, the game had been over, above two minutes, and repeated calls for "time" had been made by the spectators. Curiously enough, immediately the visitors scored, the referee blew his whistle for the ceontion.
PROMOTION FOR 14.11 q. T. it if A.RDY, OF WARRINGTON.

Mr. Thomas H. Hardy, who has for many years been actively engaged as secretary to the St. John Ambulance Corps in Warrington, left Warrington on Tuesday to undertake new duties as inspector of waggons for the Great Central Railway at Frod- dinghara, North Lincolnshire. Mr. Hardy has been employed at the Central Station in the waggon de- partment for the past nine years, and has been very popular among his fellow-servants at the station. He was an enthusiastic ambulance min, and it was largely owing to his exertions that Fomo years ago a corps was formed in Warrington. He was ap- pointed hon. secretary and superintendent of stores. The corps increased in membership, and a brigade was formed, which alone has over 100 members. It is now in an exceedingly flourishing state. The news of the departure of Mr. [lardy has been re- ceived with much regret. both by the ambulance men and the railway men of the town, though the regret has been intermingled with satisfaction that he has received promotion.

div.head: MAN OUT AHEAD.
div.p: THE MAN OUT AHEAD.

The man with oil aid smut on his pa!mi, and per. haps a touch of it on his nose; the an who never rides first-class, tut always riclfs first—a class all of himself : if, when starting out on a railway journey, you havo any thoughts or prayers not immediately re. quired for your own use, invest them in him.

For although the p?sseagers oa the train may ba plentifully punctuaed with princes and ciuk.es, capitals ists, promoter, M P.'s bishops, and other clergy, plug liberat spooniuls of ne very cream of society, neverthed less the man with the grease aid coal dust on hitn is far and away tne most important fellow on board.

When the present writer sink back into he soft era- brace of a seat ia a coach of a fast exp •ess for Liverpool and seas, as he lights his pipe, the platforms of Eustos Station swim away,be never fails t t Ike a mental snap* shot at the Man on the Machine ; for whether we rug into the big shed at Lime-Areot or into the bigger shed of Eternity, depends largely on him. Sober he will be. May he also be heathy an I hearty, elEar-eyed, cool, and steady. For in the hollow of his grimy band be holds us all.

One of these men, Mr. Thomas Wilkinson, is—and for many years his been—in the employ of the L. and N.W. Railway. He is (almost needless to say) competent and fortunate. Otherwise he could not have retained bift position. The line has suffared no serious calamity for which he could be btld tespcnsible. Scmetimas b would be laid up for a fetv days, but that was his bai luck—not that of the company or of the public. For, look you ! important as it is thlt engine driveni should be sound men, they are not necessarily so. If it were a hard and fast rule that men who run locomotive should never be ill, especially when on duty the volume of traffic would fall off materially. As iosn do other kinds of work when half ill, so they are obliged to drive the iron horse in the same condition. Pilots of steam boats and wheelsmea on ships hive thopped dead at their posts ; and the faithful chaps on the reeling stean2 wa,,oas are not exempt from the common fate.

" For over 26 years," says Mr. Wilkinson-,-;; I was go° no times a really well man. I had ircquent spells of giddiness and pain in the back of the head. I had alSo a bad taste in thu mouth, a poor appei:e, and after eats ing wy food often' repeate.l,' or ca me up in my throat. There was much pin at my chest and stomach, al though what I ate stopped there, like a train sliunted oft the main line.

" What W 3,8 particularly bid for /113 was loss of sleep more or lesi, at night ;so that I felt tired and out of coalition in the morning. In the course of time I got weak and found it hari to get on with my duty. Hoyt' ever, I struggled on as I could, aril came through all right,but the strain was all I wantel Co stand up under. " Smnetimes when I rained home after a day's run I was so worn out and exhausted that I was glad tO settle down anywhere."

"1 consulted doctors and took many different /medi• clues, but only got ease for the time. Then the com- plaint came on again bad as ever. So it was with ine —up and down, but never well or right. " I had often heard of Mother Seigel's Syrup as a sure remedy for ineigestion and chronic dyspepsia, but up to this tim 3 had not enough faith in it to try it. In Novera‘ ber. 1885, I read about it; I mean cases it bad cured' some worse than mine-

"On this I bought a battle from Mr. F. W. EfugheSt The Inca Drug Stores, Spring View, Lower Inc', sad it did me a lot of good. I kept on taking it, anl it waso'd long before 1 enj )yod my meals and everything agreed with me. The pain in the head and the giddiness tron, blei me no more, and I was another man. I only re. gretted not having kno 'en of Mother Seigel's Syrup 20 years before. I tried Mother Seigel's Soothing Plateril for pain in the aids and ba ck, and they relieved me Dv stantly.

"1 tsli all my friends abut bowl was cured,and yots may feel at liberty to publish my hasty letter if yoo think it may prove uslfu I. I will reply to any inquiries.' (Signed) THOILIS WEL KINSON, 258, Warrington-roadi Lower lace, Near Wigan, Lanes. Nov. 11th, 1898.

WYCLIFFE COCIMEDGE MISSION.
ANNUAL TEA. MEETING AND PRESENTATION.

There was a large attendance at the annual Congrega- tional t.a meeting in connection with Wycliffe Cock- hedge Mission held OR Monday evening. The event was additionally interesting on account of a presentation to Mr. John Plinston, the superintendent of the Mission,on the occasion of his marriage and the severance of his connection with the Mission due to his removal to the Isle of Man. Tea was served in the schoolroom, and the subsequent proceedings were held in the Mission, pre- sided over by the Rev. John Yonge. The CHAIRMAN in his opening remarks thought there were many grounds for congratulation and `rejoicing on the past year's work at the Mission. Whatever might have been their experiences as individuals during the past twelve months, there had been most encouraging features in connection with the Sundae school and mis- sion work. They had occasion to thank God for the past and take courage fr the future. (Rear, hear.) Mr. B. HALL, one of the secretaries of the Mission presented the annual report. They started last year with a great deal of work before them and he was glad to be able to state that they had succeeded in accom- plishing their aims. A new class room had been pro- vided which would greatly assist them in their Sunday school work, and the long-felt want of a good musical instrument to assist them in their services had been supplied by the provision of an organ. Their labours in connection with both the mission and school had been attended with success. Some of their number had joined the church and they contemplated others during the coming year. The Christian Endeavour Society, the working classes, and the other organisations in connec- tion with the Mission were in a very healthy condition. In conclusion he appealed for more workers to make their institutions a still greater success. (Applause.) Mr. PEERS reported on the work of the local preach- ers who had assisted at the services, and said they owed a debt of gratitude to those who bad so freely and generously given of their services. Mr. ROGER presented the report of the Sunday schoJl. stating that the number of scholars was 375, and the teachers numbered 19. He pointed out that Mr. Plias- ton, who was new leaving them, was one of a number who came from Wycliffe to the mission more than 23 years ago to assist in the work of the Sunday school. The mission school was now able to provide almost a 1 ' its teachers.
WORTH A GUINEA A BOX.

The CHAIRMAN said the next item was a presentation to Mr. John Plinston. (Applause.) There was no one in connection with the mission whom he held in higher steem than their friend who was ending his work in their midst that day. The service Mr. Plinston had ren- dered in connection with Cockhedge Mission and Sunday school haa been of a most devoted and unselfish charac- ter. He thought it would he a difficult matter to find a successor who would be willing to do all Mr. Plinston had done. Amidst the congratulations they offered him, and amidst all the good wishes they felt and ex pressed towards him for the years which might be to come it was only natural and perfectly unavoidable that they who were left behind felt considerable regret in bidding him farewell. (Applause.) Mr. MAYBURY was then called upon to make the pre- sentation. consisting of a handsome silver urn and a purse of money. In doing so Mr. Maybury referred in a humorous vein to his long association with Mr. Pens- ton personally and in the work of the mission. He pro- ceeded to state that when it became known Mr. Plinston was about to leave them, a committee was formed repre- sentative of the several organisatiors in connection with the Mission, and a subscription list was started. After paying for the urn the balance was turned into gold. It was now his pleasure in the name of the Mission, the friends at Wycliffe, and the organisations cennected with the Mission to make the Ines: ntatien. The urn bore the following inscription :—" Presented to Mr. John Plinston for 23 years' faithful services at Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission, Warrineton, on the °cession of his marriage,February 27th, 1899." (Applause.) Mr. JACKSON then handed a purse of gold to Mr. Plinston. He wished Mr. and Mrs. Marlton very much happiness, and lsop-ct they would live long to enj.ry their wedded life. (Applause.) Mr. PLINSTON who was very cordially received,thanked the subscribers for their handsome gilts, and the speaker for their kindly remarks. He had fell-, for many years that the people connected with 'Cockhedge valued his services and he had done his utmost to make the mission a success. He wi9hed to thlok the workers for the hearty manner in which they had supported him. That was the last night he stod before them as a worker at the Mission but ~he hoped they would be spared to see each other again. (Applause.) Mr. THOMAS HAWTHORN then prene nted the financial statement of the eliese:n which showed a very satis- factory state of affairs. Toe improvem-nts had been paid for, and an organ purchased, and yet there was only a deficit of is 61 at the end of the year. In con- elusion he paid a tribute to Mr. PlinAon's services to the Mission.

Toe services of these who had assisted during the evening were acknow- ledged on the proposition of Mr. Holland seconded by Mr. North.

div.head: EmmmunoNAL PEACE CRUSADE.
div.p: EmmmunoNAL PEACE CRUSADE.

Sir.—We have been requested coact as hon. secretaries and hon. tressurer, for this district in connecti3n with this important movement. It is now well known that the Czsr's proposA conference receives the support of not only all our prominent leaders,whether in religion or politics, but also of all thoughtful and humane persons. It ought to be universally underst33d that this is not a Peace-at-any-price movement ; that there is no desire for any one-s ded arrest in the :increase of armaments ; Still less of any one-sided dirninurion. What it is hoped may, among other things, be acc-mplishel at the International Conterence is.

1. That nations may be induced to submit their differenc:!s to same recognised court of arbitration not instead ef fighting,but beil)re fighting. In many ewes as already sJea in the industrial sphera, internecine strife might be averted. a That more humane cmditions may be suggegted under which war when it is unhappily thought to be necessary, might be conducted. 3. That military op: rations s'aoulki be confined as

much as possible t; the armies engaged, and so, much of the havoc, distress, and disorganisation among the civil population avoided. 4. 'nut some practical plan should be discussed whereby the retire increase of armaments might be generally a rlest ed. The expenditure of the principal powers of Europe on their armies and navies has increased since 1870 from 104 millions to 202 millions—and the Britisa from 22 to 44 raiilions. I tlit-res to be no limt? There are many people who s fail to think that war and tht preparation of war is good for trade. This economic fallacy' is an old eae and dies hard. Mere expenditure of m,,ney is not good for trade as a whole. Only money spent pr3ductively is good for trade as a whole. Thc fallacy is sugge ,tive of the undergraduate's essay an the Shetlanders, whom he described as earning a precarious livelihood by washing one another's clothes. If as the only outcome of this unique movement there be but the growth of a nebler conception of our duty as parts of the great family of nations,it will not have been in vain. Lord Salisbury in his reply to the Russian gov2rnment, has intimated his sense of the great useful- ness of this agitation in order to convince the various governments that the people are really in earnest in this matter.

Volunteers my be ennlied ; the Czar's memorial signed, and Crusicte bacl4e2, omained f• om Mr. Dlvil- son, (late Lowe and Laituwait-), 61, Bridge-szreet.
