div.head: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.

The annual general meeting of the members of the Earlestown Cricket Club was he'd in an ante-room of the Viaduct Institute on Monday evening. Mr. T. Ormand presided, but owing to overtime being worked in the Viaduct Works, there waq only a moderate attendance. The Secretary (Mr. J. Owen) read the annual report which was as follows :

"For a number os years past it has invariably been our pleasure at these annual gatherings to speak of the steady progress we were making, but in looking over a cutting from one of our local papers publishers at the close of last season, lam reminded that the averages then pre- sented were the worst since the club was instituted. , Perhaps it would hardly be correct to accept this state- 'meet literally, for those of us whose memories Can take them back some 14 or 15 years will remember how diffi- cult it was to exist, let alone make any progress, but certain it is that since we were established on a firm footing, it has not fallen to my lot to present a more un- favourable report. However, as you have often been re- minded, we must be prepared for bad as well as goad seasons, and though we ca ;net congratulate ourselves upon this cccasion, we can at any rate look the year which is before us, in the face, determined to meke it more profitable than its prerleceeser.Our prosiamme con- sisted of 21 matches. 4 of these were cancelled owing to the wet weather, and unfortunately 3 of them.St.flolens Rea% Newton and Burslern, should have been played on their own ground ; of the remaining games, 5 only were won, 10 lost, and 2 drawn. Once only did victory smile upon us at home, so that our supporters had little to coneele themselves with. Two records were estab- lished to our discomfort, one being at Eerlestown on July 9th, when Cheetnam dismissed us for 26; the other at Manchester a fortnight later, the home players scoring no less tha s 452 runs for 6 wickets. These however are by no means the only instances when our men failed to do themselves justice. We entered _upon the season without professional aid, deciding to rely principally upon our own young players. This would probably have worked out advantageously had we not bad the misfortune to lose the services of two of the most pro- minent bowlers. R. Bell, for almost the whole of the season, and J. H. Alderson, for fully half of the matches. Despite these drawbacks, several of the players c,aim to have made some progress, Hue- baud, Mitchell. Foreman and Crowther have improved in betting and James Hatton and Hipwool have ad- vanced in bowling. 1717 runs were scored for 157 wick( ts, averaging 10.147, our cppenent4 totalled 2653 runs for 149 wickets, or an average of 17120. In the previous rear the average number of runs scored by us was 12 140 per wicket, that of our opponents being 14.104, so that the comparison is to our disadvantage in I both cases. It is with satisfaction that we have to refer to the doings of the second eleven. Whilst the seniors could hardly de the right thing, they were carrying al- most ail before them, losing two matches only, through- out the year: Their success was wit due to any indivi- dual effort, but to the team as a whole, as a reference to the published figures show 10 members to have aver- ages of 14 and upwards, while the five leading bowlers are all under 9 runs per wicket. With these facts before us it seems strange that successful recruits could not be discovered for the first eleven, and as 21 players were tried in the premier team the fault can hardly be urged against your Came:et:Fie. that they failed to provide now blood, bat rather that the men themselves have not vet fitted themselves for the better clase of cricket demanded from them. It is chiefly on this account that a new departure is isbeut to be made this year. The services of a professional have been engaged, whose duty it will be to coach the young players. and train them to t-ks their place and assist to bring the club back to the position it held some few years ago. Ira connection with this new arrangement we are looking forward to an improvement in thequalitv of the ground; we hope to find the wickets here in the future at least equal to these of the club; we visit. As in former years the Institute Committee generously provided four hats for competition in addition to a sum of £2. Messrs. Husband, Alderson, (Amend and James Hatton have been awarcle 1 the hats for heading the batting and bowline averages in their respective teams. Messrs. Mitchell, Hipwood, Dev:es and Wainwright receive goods to the value of 10r. each as our committee deem them to be tbe next in order or merit. Home and home matches have been arraneed with Ceeetham. Blacklev, Wigan. Leigh,Liverpeol, Tyldesley, Se Helene, and St Helens Recs, one match at Earlestown with Manchester and one with 18 juniors of the dierict. The financial statement which I have to present shows the amount of cash reeeive i from all sources to be £47 133 91 and the expenditure. including a balance which was due to the Tr^aaurer at the cemmencement of tee season of £44 2.3 81 leaving £3 lie idle the Treasurer's hands. Taking into consideration that we had no professional fees to pay, this does not appear to be a large amennt to have an hand. As a set off ageinst this the gate receipts were very low compared with former years in consequence of the vary wet season, the cancelling of three of the most attractive matches meant the loss of several pounde.TtlA expensive nature of our out matches has been the rn,ans rf adding £2 to the players ex- Penises, no lege a sum than £l4 Us 81 being spent under this head. We are committed to a much larger ou'lay in the enpreashing season toi meet this we are looking for an increased attendance at the m echo as well at an addition to rho membership. The professional help which it was deemed necessary to provide will, we hope,enabla us to give abetter account of ourselver. It has frequently been remarked th it our members would be augmented if this course were adopted, and as 44 per annum is all that is revived from members, we tenet that many will be prevailed upon to join us in our eff art to make the club worthy oh the .town we live in. (Applause.) The Chairman said it. was gratifying to notice that they had a balance in hand of £3 Us 11 which would have been greater had the gate receiots been as much as in Twit years, in one year they had reached as much as £2l. The exlearditure ha; been very carefully watched by the Committee, otherwise they would have had a halenee on the wrong side again. The Institute Cam- mines were spiring no eff arts to make the ground one of the beet in this part of the country, and they hoped to make it equal to any gronad in Lancashire. He might tell them that on Friday last the Committee in its endeavour to siintelate the physical welfare of the members not of the Cricket Club alone; but of the who'e of its mernbere.voten two-thirds gate money to the elle,. and £2 for nrizee to b awarded for bats etc., and £lO. towards the, expense; which would be incurred by the engagement of a professional cricketer, and ran effort; wield be wanting on the part of the Crommiqee and members to make the club a success in the coming year. (Applause.) The Secretary's report and balance sheet ware adop- ted.

div.head: VOTES OF THANTCS.
div.p: VOTES OF THANTCS.

The Secretary thought it would be better if a vote of thanks went from th it meeting to the Institute Com- mittee for their genercsity in assisting the Club. For many years past till members had been indebted to them, and had it not been for the Committeethey would not now be in existeace. Everything that the Club had asked for had been granted, velich showed that the Institute Committee were se anxious to further the intlrests of the club, as the club itself was. He had pleasure in movine a vote of thanks to the Committee for what they had done. Re %vas delighted with the amount of their vnerosity, and it would be a shame if the young members did not show their appreciation of it, and do their utmoftt. He had seen the time when they were in the habit of getting hold 2f players when- ever they could. There used to be a great deal of enthu- siasm, and now they had determined to rely upon their young blood, there did not seem to be that enthusiasm and he did not think it was right, as they ought to do their best to get out of the ace md team and into the first. There was no club which had the some chance or working on such a cheap scale, nor which btad the same advantages as they had. (Applause). Mr. Liversage in seconding, corroborated all that bad been said. Mr. Roberts supported and the motioa was put and 'tarried. Mr. Ormand, as secretary of the listitute Committee said, that although they did no k for any such ex- pression as they had sbnyen, s9ll he was sure they would appreciate whet had been said. div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY Kr EA.RLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY Kr EA.RLESTOWN.
(BY A CORRESPONDENT.)

The Council have generously decided to make an abatement on the bills of gas consumers for the quarter ending December last, at the rate of ten per cent. Tnis is as it ought to be, and shows at once those who have paid the demands have really paid for something they have not had. It is no use cri- ticising any further the point relating to over pres- sure for the benefit oF one particalar consumer, see- ing that the Council have acted honourably in the matter. At the same time one cannot help feeling that whilst the committee who had the question in hand were considering it, they might have come to some decision about the quality of the.gas. That is a very sore point, for the lighting quality is as bad as it well Can be at the price. Perhaps, how- ever, the new Gas and Water Engineer may intro- duce something which will improve the present condition of things. It is to be hoped he will, and in that event we can wait patiently.

The lecture given last week on "The British Empire" was perhaps the most interesting of any which has yet been given under the auspices of the Lectures C3mmittee. The subjects for the remainder of the course are very attractive, and will thubtlesg prove as interesting as the opening lecture. To my mind such lectures are just as profitable, and o as much advantage t 3 the inhabitants as the purely scientific discburs-s to which we have hitherto been treated. Geography is always an interesting subject, and in this enene!tilti I consider history holds an equal place. I would theref3re urge up3n the committee when considering the arrangements to be made for the next session, that the qmstion of a historicil course, receives a first place in their deliberations.

The Peace Crusade meeting WA4 very sparsely attended indeed, but as it was state'], doubtless this was due, not to any lack of sympathy with the sub- ject, hut to the fact that the majority ot the work- ing classes were working overtime. Some of the speeches were good and to the point, but the Rw. F. A. Mitchell rather wandered away from the sub- ject, and it was difficult at times to see what con- nection his tirade on religion had with the objects of the meeting, A. good many also, were doubtless disappointed at the oratory of the Rev. A. N Elliott who came down specially to educate the people on the =atter, but his style of delivery was not of the kind to rouse enthusiaim, nor were his arguments in all cases connective or eftictiva. The audienc., however, gathered saffi-_;ient from what was said to enable them to pass the resolution wilich was put before them.

Thursday. next week, is the date set apart for the receipt of nominations for a Councillor in al the five Wards in the township. Of course there are various rumours afilat ai to contests, but how far these will turn out to be correct I am at present unable to say. I think it is pretty certlin, however, that there will be a cante4t in the Viaduct Ward, where Mr. P. McMahon's term expires. Mr. F. C;arke aspires to Council honours. and it is he who will make a bid for Viaduct Ware on the day of election. I have hear-I a rumur of a contest in Town Hall Ward, but there is no authoritative con- firmation of it. In the other Wards there will be no contests.

The Earlestown Cricket Club held their annual meeting on Monday night and the Secretary in his report rather gloomily referred to the very bad season the club had experienced. This, he ex- plained, was due to a variety of causes, chief amongst which was the weather, for on three.occa- sloes when it might relsonably be expected there would be large gates, the rain came down piteously and placed all idea of cricket beyond question. He referrei in hopeful terms to the coming season, commenting upon the fact that a Drifessional had been engaged, who would considerably, it was hoped, augment the strength of the club. There/ are plenty of young and promising players in the club and it is thoug'it with the assistance of the pro- fessional they may blasenm forth into something beyond the " promising "stage.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Earlestown Linda narrow squeak on Saturday. The match was against Bamfurlong Rovers, in the Wigan Cup Competition. and as this was the third time the teams had met considerable interest was taken in the contest. If the spectators went to see football, they were grievou4ly mistaken, hut if they fully expected to see a melee, then they got their money's wlrth. There was altogether too much feeling thrown into the game, and as was to be ex- pected, there was altogether an entire absence of good football.

Both teams were equilly to blame, and it needed all the firmness at the command of the referee t ) keep the game going. Leach early on in the game had a splendid opportunity to open the scoring, but hi, anxiety to collide with an opponent, diverted his attention from the ball and so be lost his chance. The Bamfurlong team was much more dangerous in front of goal than the home forwards, and they deserved to win if only for the brilliance of their attack. Their back division worked well, but the home backs were a source of trouble and anxiety to Chew the home castolian. The dangerous rushes of the visiting forwards completely upset the calcu- lations of Wilkinson and Hayes, who failed on several ocoaiions to repel the attack. Not only s 2, but through Idling back on the goal, they con- siderably hampered Chew, who should have been viven plenty of liberty of action. His brilliant goal keeping saved disaster, but if the home backs played with mor..J calculation and dash, they would net only assist Chew in keeping his charge intact, but would render the task of the forwards more easy.
On Saturday, Earlest-own are at horn 3 to S. Helens Recs., in an Alliance fixture, whea it is hoped that there will be a large crawd.

The Earlestown Rovers visited Richrnonds at Warrington in the Warrington and District Leia,czne and succeedel in defeating them by 5 goals to nil.

St JOEIN'S Cittraca SUNDA.Y SCITOOL,EARLICSTOWN On Monday eveniog the annual distribution o awards to the scholars attending the above, and Mission School, took place in the Mission Hall. There were very few besides the prize winners, pre- sent. The Rev. F. C. Shirteldle, curate, presided in the unavoidable absence of the Vicar, who was in- disposed. Toe chairmAn said that prize day WAS a very important day, and was always looked forward to by scholars with joyful expectation. Generally, most boys and girls, :strove hard to earn a prize and he hoped when they obtained them they were ap- preciated. He (.the curate), during the course of his visitations in the parish, had been shown by parents prizes which had been obtained in the Sun- day school by their children. This showed they were proud of them. He hoped they would not only strive for prizes, but also reepect their teachers who kindly gave their time and abilities for their good, and if they respected their teachers they would also respect the Great Teacher of all, the blessed Lord Jesus Christ. (Applause.) The secretary (Mr. T. Martindale) submitted a report of the schools in which he said the namb,er of scholars on the books was 1,015, including 110, in the young men's and married men's classes. The average attendance was 813, or 80 per cent. The number of teachers was 45, with an average attendance of 40. The Mission Hall had again been opened for some months,under the euperintennence of Mr. liaison, and he was I pleased to state that the number of scholars was 110 with eight teachers. There were to be distributed that night 81 books to the scholars of the Parish Church schools and 19 to the Mission Hall school children, for regular attendance and good conduct. The financial statement showed that after the pay- ment of all expenses there was a balance in hand of .£1 18e &id: The prizes were afterwards distributed by the Rev. F, C. Shirtcliffe. During the evening a programme of instrumental and vocal music was given by scholars and members of the choir. " LIN3BBD COMPOUND" for Coughs and Colds, Asthmaand Bronchitis. Of Chemists only.—Advt.

div.head: LATE MR. P. E. SCOTT.
div.p: THE LATE MR. P. E. SCOTT.

It is with deep regret that we have to record the death of Mr. Percival B. Scott, the Liberal candi- date for Warrington at the last general election. Mr. Scott had been in a delicate state of health for a number of years, and at the time of his visit to Warrington was hardly in a coaditioa to undergo the strain of an uphill Parliamentary- contest. His death took place on Friday, last week, at the house of his sister, New Holme,Goulden-road. Withington, but news of the sad event was not received in War- rington until Monday evening, and was not generally knowa until the following day. Expressions of sorrow have been heard on all hands since, and there has been abundant evid- ence of the warm esteem in which Mr. Scott was held by all those who worked for him and voted for him in July 1895. Mr. Scott was only 32 years old, and tell a victim to consumption. He was born in 1867 and was the son of Mr. Thomas Bell Scott, of Manchester, in which city he was born, and was up to a few months ago the m inagin;,7 director of the wholesale and retail firm of Messrs. John Satterfield and Co., of S. Aan'.i-square, Manchester, silk mer- chants and drapers. On Seurdey, July 6th, 1895, Mr. Scott was formally adepted es the Liberal Can- didate in opposition to Mr. R. Pierpoint. The elec- tion took place on Monday, July 15th, when Mr. Scott was defeated by 675 votes,the number of votes recorded for each candidate being : Pierpoint, 4,001 Scott, 3,326. In the nine days intervening between his adoption as Liberal candidate and the poll Mr. Scott had to make himself known to his constitu- ents and secure their support—en almost super- human task. He faced it with indomitable pluck, addressed meeting after meeting. canvassed the town, and altogether made such efforts that he was ultimately enabled te record more votes than any previous Liberal candidate—a fact which speaks volumes for his poenalarity,aed the earnestness with which he threw himself into the fray. The decease 1 gentleman ingratiated himself with the electors in an astonishingly short space of time. Few men have a greater charm of manner than he had, and his eloquent addresses always aroused the utmost enthusiasm. Had the time not been so short it is quite possible that Mr. Scott would have been successful, but though de- feate Ihe was not disheartened, and after the poll expressed his confidence in being able to win the seat on the next occasion. His bodily frailty, how- ever, compelled him to give up thoughts of ever entering the lists again, and since the election in 1895 he has been seldom seen in the town. Perham the most recent cccasion on which he was in Warrington was at the the funeral of the late Mr. Thomas Morris. The exacting nature of public life, and his physical inability to endure it, have been the causes leading to the practical sever- ance of Mr. Scott's cannection with Warrington. The decease from which he suffered gradually over- came him, and he died,as stated.to the great sorrow of all who knew him. THE FUNERAL.

It was the requst of Mr. Scott and his relatives that the funeral should be a private one, otherwise, Ardwick Cemetery, where the deceased was in- terred on Tuesday afternoon, would undoubtedly have been the scene of a large gathering of sym- pathetic friends. The attendance included in addi- tion to a few friends : Ar T k Scott f,brother), Mr IT Russell (brother-in-law) Mr Vernon (from Messrs Sendai, Milne, and Co.), Mr. Henry Roberts (hon. secretary of the Warrington Liberal Association), Mr W'rurness(bon.treas.of the Liberal Association) and Mr D Tinnion (chairman of the Liberal Club.) The coffin was of English polished oak, with brass mountings. and the inscription was as follows : "Percival Brown Scott, died on the February 1899, aged 32 years." The first part of the funeral service was conducted at th,l house by the deceased's own pastor of the Nonconformist Church, the Rev. Mr. Slater, and the reverend gentleman concluded the last sad rites at the graveside, where a large number of floral wreaths bore eloquent tribute to the regard with which the deceased had been everywhere held. Among many others there were wreathe from Warringt om Liberal Association, Warrington Liberal Club, and Mr. A. H. Crosfield.

div.head: PROSPECTUS OF" TITAN "SOAP, LIMITED.
div.p: PROSPECTUS OF" TITAN "SOAP, LIMITED.

We publish in another colutan the prospectus of a company to be known in future as "Titan "Soap Limited, which has been formed for the purpose of acquiring, as a going concern, the well-known busi- ness formerly carried on by the Liverpool Patent Soap Company, at Liverpool, with all rights and in- terest in the celebrated brand and trade mark " Titan " patent soap; all rights and interest in a patent granted to Thomas Arthur Myers relating to the packing of liquid soap, and the extensive free- hold-property formerly known as Messrs. Medley and Sons' Soap Works, Naylor-street, Liverpaol. The capital of the company is £05,000 divided into 30,000 per cent cumulative preference shares of .E 1 each, and 35,000 ordinary shares of £1 each. " Titan " soap was placed on the market in July 1890, and its ready sale may judged by the fact that 12,000 accounts have already been opened. Over £55,000 has been spent in advertising the soap, and its name is known far and wide. By a new process under Mr. Myers' patent, the soap can now be sup- plied in a liquid form enclosed in rigid soluble capsules which immediately dissolve on immersion in hot water and give, at once, the best results. The works are centrally situate, within six minutes walk of the Liverpool Exchange, close to the railway goods stations and in proximity to the line of docks. They are capable of turning out 120 tons of soap per week. It is estimated that a factory of a similar character could not be erected and fitted to-day at a cost of less than £21,000. Messrs. Voisey and Worthington, of Warrington have examined the books of the Liverpool Patent Slap Company, and those relating to: the manufac- ture of" Titan" Sosp for the three years ended 31st Decembar, 1897, and certify that the net profits hare been £15,171 23 6d. This is an average of £5,057 Os 101 per anuum, and after paying a divi- dend on the preference shares would leave a balance of £3,407 Os 10(1 for dist!ibution amongst the or- dinary shareholders. This computation does not take any account of the largely increased profits that are anticipated from the extension of the com- pany's operations. In addition to making "Titan" Soap it is intended to fully eqaip the works with the most modern machinery and appliances for the manufacture of other descriptions of household and laundry soaps. The price to be paid by the company for the var;ous assets, &c., is £48,000. The £17,000 remaining from the preezit issue will be set aside for additional working capital. The list will open on Monday the 6th of March, and close on or before the Wednesday following.
NEWTON DEBATING tOCIETY.

The usual weekly meeting of this Scciety was held in the Congregational Sctioolro(im on Monday evening. Mr. W. Speakman presidvd, The pro- gramme was "Readings and Recitations from various authors." Several of the members contribu- ted interesting items from their favourite authors, and a profitable evening was spent. GAS AND WATER ENGINEER FOR NEWTON.

In response to the advertisement for a Gas and Water Engineer for the Urban District of Newton- in-Makerfield, 34 applications have la,.ien received. A Sub-Committee sat on Monday, and selected five applicants to appear before the Committee on Mon- day. and it is expected the final selection will then be made.

I was told that Alfred Rayner had passed standard IV, but this did not take Disc at any of my inspections. All four boys now at full time labeur (and therefore not attending school) are too young to have been taken away from school." Admiral Jones Parry sa7d the explanation would come. under the House Committee's report. , In sudrnitting the IleerFe Committee's rsport the Marie ter said it was a mistake due to the boy Alfred Hughes. being also known as Alfred ,Raynor.

ALLEGED SACRILEGE AT A. V A.RRING TON CHURCH. A MAN IN CUSTODY. On Friday, at the Warrington Borough Polic Court, before the Mayor (Alderman Wright) and ether magistrates, a resptchbly dressed man about 40 years of age,who gave the name of amid. Davies Iv!tii charged with stealing from the charity con tribution box about 3 o'clock on Thursday after- noon, a sum of money, the amount unknown, the Property of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church trus- tees. The Chief Constable said he would ask for a re- ?and of the prisoner in order to make inquiries. he prisoner was cilarged with breaking open a ontributiou box in St. Mary's Catholic Church, Intermarket-street, and stealing therefrom a sum cl money unknown. it appeared that about three °clock Mr. John Eckersley went into the orgrn loft to play the organ and whilst there he heard n.olses of splintering wood and the chink- .,lng of money. Being suspicious Air. Eckers- ley came hastily downstairs and notic.Fd that one cf the charity boxes had been broken open and the 'wood scattered on the floor. The piisoner was ittanding close to the box and on seeing Mr, -ctokersley he made an effort to hastily leave the .entirch. Mr. Eckersley detained him and sent for e police. Superintendent Monaghan went to the to!irchand received the prisoner into custody. On Ping searched a screw-driver, a strong knife, a .Rtrelet, and a number 01 keys which were obviously Church keys were found upon the prisoner. He also ad between £4 and £5 in money, a Watch, and seemed well provided with this orld's goods. At the railway station the prisoner ad a parcel containing a new suit of clothes. He tefused to give any account of himself, end it was that morning he had given the name of Daniel ~Tlvies.—The defendant said be would like to have "e matter settled now.—The magistrates decided to remand him for seven days.

Richards, rdills and Company, managers of the Dominion Steamship Line, whose headquarters are at Liverpool, have received a message stating that their ship, the Labrador, went ashore at Skerryvore, in the Hebrideniat 7 a.m. on We:ineselay but that no lives have been lost. The message, which is from the captain,Mr. T. W. Erskine, is as follows :—"Labrador, during thick fog, ran on the Mackenzie Rock at 7 a.m. yesterday,four miles from Skerryvore Lighthouse. She struck the rock amidships, and the sea i 3 breaking over her. One, two, and three holds ara full of wafer. Paaaengers and crew were all saved, and left the ship in boats. One boat with passengers landed at the lighthouse. All the ether boats were picked up by the German steamer Viking. If the ship does not break no I will endeavour to save mails.' MR. RUDYARD KIPLING.
